This figure is consistent with existing predictions from the Standard Model, which forecast an value of 1.497 picoseconds for this parameter. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. A key aspect of this problem is the presence of the control variable in the diffusion term, which poses challenges for standard finite element methods, yet can be addressed through a combination of continuous and discrete solutions using the Lagrange formalism and the Monte-Carlo method. Moreover, it demonstrates the convergence of this combined approach, thereby establishing the mathematical framework for solving an instance of the problem numerically, which involves solving a nonlinear problem with a complex diffusion coefficient affected by the control variable, both analytically and numerically, and ultimately establishes the convergence of a specific numerical scheme when the Monte-Carlo method is combined with the finite element method. Furthermore, it numerically solves a stochastic control problem where the diffusion coefficient varies significantly and has a nonlinear impact on the solution, and presents the results of this numerical solution, thereby validating the effectiveness of this combined numerical solution approach. In addition, it also compares the performance of different numerical schemes for solving this particular problem, which can be used as a benchmark for similar numerical schemes, and provides the source code of the numerical solutions for replication purposes. In addition, it also considers a more general instance of the problem where the objective functional involves a term that represents the expectation of a maximum or a minimum value, which can be approximately solved using the Monte-Carlo method, and presents the results of this approximation, thereby validating the effectiveness of this approximation method. Finally, it also considers a more challenging instance of the problem where the domain is divided into multiple sub-domains, which adds an additional layer of complexity, and presents the results of this numerical solution, which demonstrates the convergence of the combined numerical solution approach when the number of sub-domains increases, and provides the source code of the numerical solutions for replication purposes. This research paper is particularly relevant to researchers and scientists within the field of applied mathematics, specifically in the areas of stochastic control theory, numerical solution of partial differential equations, and scientific computing, and which has implications for real-world applications in fields such as finance, navigation, and optimization processes. This paper is also relevant to anyone seeking to understand the Monte-Carlo method and the finite element method, which are widely used numerical solution techniques, and which can be used to solve this particular instance of the problem

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our observations underscore the necessity for a comprehensive explanation of cosmic ray anisotropies that considers both the origins of these high-energy particles and the cosmic magnetic fields through which they traverse en route to Earth. Given the enhanced resolution of anisotropy patterns enabled by the expanded layout of the Pierre Auger Observatory, we anticipate that future discoveries will build upon this study, potentially revealing small-scale anisotropies in cosmic rays at the highest energy levels. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. The paper also provides an example demonstrating that there are infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras with specific properties, such as being nilpotent and having a specific dimension, over any field in its finite characteristic, yet these do not coincide with Lie algebras. The paper further investigates graded and periodic Zinbiel algebras, establishing that they are nilpotent with a gradeable nilpotency structure, and also finds the basis for their nilpotency characterizing it as periodic with a gradeable structure. The paper additionally constructs and examines a specific family of non-Lie Zinbiel algebras, known as the Witten algebras, which arise in string theory, revealing that these algebras are nilpotent of a specific order, with a gradeable nilpotency structure, and also possess a periodic property for grades greater than two. The paper further delves into finding the basis for these Witten algebras, providing valuable insights into its structure and character. The paper also explores and establishes relationships between the nilpotency of Witten algebras and the parameter 'h' which defines them, revealing that these algebras are solvable for any value of 'h', yet the paper fails to determine if these algebras are nilpotent for fields other than those with a finite characteristic. The paper also fails to determine if there are distinct infinite-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebras for each value of the characteristic 'char', yet it succeeds in establishing that for fields with a characteristic other than one, there are nilpotent graded Zinbiel algebras of a specific dimension, known as the 'dim' character. The paper also provides an example of a non-Lie Zinbiel algebra, known as the 'N(4)' algebra, which arises in mathematical physics, specifically in open-closed string field theory, demonstrating that this algebra is nilpotent, solvable, and has a gradeable nilpotency structure, yet the paper fails to explore its properties further. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. This landmark study paves the way for future, more comprehensive studies of particle flow's dynamics in heavy-ion collisions. Given the substantial insights it offers, this research is expected to significantly influence the development of future experiments at the LHC and other heavy-ion colliders around the world. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we showcase the applicability of our theory to practical scenarios through concrete examples. Notably, our theories can be applied to specific scenarios, such as handling null values, by incorporating additional parameters. Moreover, our query validation framework can be viewed as a blueprint for addressing other data quality assessments, including data merging, by modifying the status function and the order relation. This research's implications are particularly evident in database scenarios involving relaxed consistency constraints, such as synchronizing distributed databases, repairing inconsistent databases, and handling self-referential databases. Ultimately, this work is intended for an expert audience familiar with advanced topics in databases, particularly those involving consistency, self-referential databases, and null values. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. These empirical examples demonstrate the TV-PARX model's ability to forecast target variables with high accuracy. In contrast to constant-parameter models, the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms its counterparts in terms of forecasting performance, as measured by the mean absolute error (MAE) and the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). In particular, the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model yields significant improvements in forecasting performance for variables characterized by sudden onset shocks, such as COVID-19 cases in Italy. In these cases, the MAE and the MAPE are reduced by 24.5% and 26.6% for Italian COVID-19 cases, and by 15.7% and 17.9% for US corporate defaults, respectively. In contrast, the time-varying TV-PARX model shows only marginal improvements in forecasting performance for variables primarily affected by gradual trends. In these cases, the MAE and the MAPE are reduced by 5.5% and 6.3% for Italian COVID-19 cases, and by 3.4% and 4.5% for US corporate defaults, respectively. In addition to its forecasting capabilities, the time-varying TV-PARX model provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of count-based time series data, particularly with regard to the evolution of parameters in relation to external covariates. In this regard, we have found that the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model is particularly effective in capturing the complex dynamics of COVID-19 cases in Italy, where the model reveals the impact of various external covariates, including national holidays

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Notably, our analysis indicates that the relation often approximated as $|z_c|\approx 1.445 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ leads to an overestimation of systematic uncertainty in model dependence. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the impact of truncating the gradient expansion on the Yang-Lee edge singularity in $\phi^4$ theory is significantly less important than other systematic uncertainties for practical purposes. Our study confirms that the shape function $\rho(y)$ can be accurately captured using a single expansion up to the next-to-leading order for both $N=2, 4$. Ultimately, our findings provide a basis for further research into the Yang-Lee edge singularity in realistic QCD scenarios. Our results also compare with available numerical data from Monte Carlo simulations of $\phi^4$ theory and symmetry-breaking QCD, and suggest that the aspect ratio $|z_c|/R_\chi$ is only weakly dependent on $N$ and thus likely universal. Our work paves the way for investigating realistic QCD scenarios with multiple fermion flavors and different symmetry breaking patterns. We have further explored the aspect ratio's behavior in these more complex scenarios, which can serve as models for the Yang-Lee edge singularity in QCD itself. We have also established that the aspect ratio's value remains essentially unchanged when considering either the true vacuum or Yang-Lee edge singularities. Moreover, our analysis has revealed that the cusp-like behavior in the two-color QCD's Yang-Llee edge singularity is a short-wave length distortion caused by the relevant universality class rather than a long-wave length phenomenon. We have further investigated the edge singularity in three-dimensional $CP^1$ model, which exhibits a smooth rather than cusp-like behavior, and has been compared with the approximation based on the high-temperature expansion. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality helped us to enumerate the possible states in the "hard" regime, as well as the corresponding AMP trajectory, by analyzing the local minima of the TAP free energy. Ultimately, our approach enabled us to precisely characterize the output of the AMP algorithm in the "hard" regime, including the hidden states and the corresponding observations. Consequently, our results provided an explicit solution to the corresponding inverse problem, thereby solving the underlying synchronization or constraint satisfaction problem. Lastly, our analysis demonstrated that the AMP algorithm abruptly changes its behavior when the average degree of the random graph transitions from less than 1 to greater than 1, despite the fact that this transition occurs over an extremely narrow range, given the scale of the problem. Notably, this sharp transition was marked by a dramatic change in the output of the AMP algorithm, as well as the associated optimization landscape, despite the fact that this transition is relatively insignificant when compared to the dimensions of the matrix involved in the problem. We also observed that the output of the AMP algorithm becomes increasingly unstable and erratic in the regime known as the "condensation phase", which we previously described in greater detail. We should mention that our approach builds upon a previous study conducted by B. Collins, J. P. Cunningham, and A. S. Greene, as well as the work of M. Jalden, S. Kulkarni, and J. S. Yedida, which provided a initial interpretation of the output of the AMP algorithm in the "easy" regime. We have, however, significantly expanded upon this previous research by extending our analysis to the "hard" regime. We have also developed a novel approach to analyze the output of the AMP algorithm in the "hard" regime, which we believe offers a level of detail not previously achieved through other methods. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We further developed a new analytical approach to model the fractal scattering of light within the aerosol and a more sophisticated modelling of the system's spectral sensitivity to accommodate the wide spectral range of both the CCD detectors and the vast number of observed target stars. By incorporating all these advancements into a combined analysis framework, we significantly enhanced the precision of the model by incorporating laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra, ultimately yielding a precision of 0.01 for the aerosol depth measurement at an elevation of 1 km above sea level. We also observed the vertical distribution of aerosol depth with a higher resolution, discovering distinct layers of aerosols and estimating the aerosol optical depth at 10 specific heights up to 10 km above sea level with a precision of 0.01 for the lower atmosphere. Moreover, this technique can be used to monitor the atmospheric scattering of neutrino telescopes in the UHE band. We also applied this approach to a decade's worth of historical data from the FRAM telescope, uncovering a seasonal variation in atmospheric scattering. Additionally, we provide a realistic simulation of the technique for future telescopes in the UHE band, including the next-generation CTA, to facilitate precision atmospheric monitoring. Ultimately, this technique has the potential to revolutionize the monitoring of variable astronomical sources through stellar photometry by enabling the precise decomposition of atmospheric scattering from observed light signals. We also explored the applicability of this approach to other ground-based optical astrophysics facilities, such as the DAO 1.5-m telescope at the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics in Canada, the SARA 0.8-m and 1.0-m telescopes in the US, and the ORYWB 0.8-m telescope in Poland,

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is now publicly available on the GitHub site www.github.com/XiaoningRan/SixDOPoseEstimation.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. It
facilitates entry point interfaces for both command-line tools and Python
objects, in addition to seamless integration with scikit-learn and the
scipy optimization suite through the `scipy.optimize` module. The underlying
optimization problems are formulated using the variable number of vectors
approach, enabling the package to accommodate various default settings, custom
path length, and Newton-Conjugate Gradient methods within the built-in
solver, as well as streamlined access to weighted and diagonally structured
inverse covariance matrix definitions. The resulting inverse covariance
matrices can be further processed using embedded matrix utilities, making
GGLasso a comprehensive, self-contained solution for resolving a wide range of
inverse covariance matrix estimation tasks. The library is openly accessible
on GitHub at https://github.com/ThomasEisnerLab/GGLasso. The affiliated
test suite, along with the examples and results, is available at
https://gglasso.test ThomasEisnerLab. The documentation for the package can be
found at https://gglasso-docs.test ThomasEisnerLab. The library's name,
GGLasso, is an acronym for General Graphical Lasso. The graph underlying the
Covariance Selection model is commonly referred to as a Girolami graph, after
Girolami (2007). The term Graphical Lasso itself was coined by Friedman
(2007). The package is the result of a research project funded by the Knut and
Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The underlying research of some algorithms used in
GGLasso was supported by a research grant from the Swedish Research Council.
The package was developed in collaboration with the research group led by
Prof. Thomas B. Fied

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Overall, this most efficient method demonstrates considerable potential for improving biomolecular simulations by leveraging the accuracy of numerical solutions to stochastic equations. Through further optimization, potential applications in other molecular simulations are also proposed. Through the public release of the code, this research invites the scientific community to contribute to future improvements of the method. The source code of the most efficient method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/md-order-parameter/ode_solver. The study's findings are published in the journal Science Advances, with the article available at https://scienceadvances.org/doi/pdf/10.1126/sciadv.abc8336. Bloch School of Business and Public Management at the University of Missouri. The author would like to acknowledge the valuable input provided by Dr. John Chodera from the Sloan-Kettering Institute, Dr. David Price from the University of Warwick, and Dr. John Richards from the University of Texas at Austin. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach by applying it to real-world data, including a case study of scientific collaboration networks. Additionally, our approach can be adapted to calculate a variation of eigenvector centrality for single-layer networks, offering an alternative solution to existing linear normalization approaches. Our method offers a range of possibilities, including the evaluation of credibility networks, the identification of influential nodes within multi-layered social media networks, and the analysis of citation networks where the direction of citations varies across different fields of study. Our algorithm and associated code are available online for public use. Our research provides a foundation for further exploration of eigenvector centrality in complex networks, particularly in relation to credibility and trust. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. The $\theta$-terms also produce massive charged states that are part of the range of the effective theory, which can be understood as "twisted" versions of the infinitely numerous, lattice-like spectrum of the zero-mass charged states. These massive charged states were previously unaccounted for in the range of the effective theory and their inclusion is crucial for understanding the $\theta$-terms which cannot be described within the parameters of the low-energy effective theory alone. Instead, they require a complete understanding of the parent string theory. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the values of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor from the original Bivector components. Ultimately, this approach enables us to obtain the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations in the Newman-Penrose formalism by considering both the complex self-dual electromagnetic field and the associated null dust solutions. This review is designed for graduate-level physics students with a strong background in general relativity and the Newman-Penrose formalism. It is necessary to note that the review primarily focuses on the self-dual case, and as such, it does not address the anti-self-dual scenarios. Additionally, the notation used in this review follows the standard conventions established by Newman and Penrose. This research was previously published in the journal Annals of Physics, volume 337, and in the journal General Relativity and Gravity, volume 46, and in the journal Nuclear Physics B, Volumes 861 and 862, and in the journal Classical and Quantum Gravity, volume 30, and in the journal Physical Review D, volumes 83, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88 and in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A, and in the book 'Exact Solutions to Einstein's Equations' edited by Stephen爵. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request. Our model's potential limitations include its reliance on large datasets and memory-intensive processing. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, descriptions on micropayment platforms might serve as a benchmark for generating similar descriptions at a lower cost. Furthermore, we could utilize less precise reference data for system fine-tuning and more rigorous evaluation against such standards. Ultimately, our goal should be to ensure that the descriptions used for evaluation reflect the actual descriptions users require and are feasible to generate with current technologies. If we prioritize reference data quality too heavily, we risk the system being inferior to those we aim to regulate. Consequently, we must be cautious when utilizing description data and continuously assess its suitability for changing societal needs. If we adhere to the current guideline rigorously, I predict it will result in systems that accurately describe the background in images, yet fail to describe the primary subject. Therefore, we need more flexible guidelines that enable system descriptions to accurately capture the substance of images by categorizing them. For this purpose, I propose a straightforward, empirically-based method to categorize image descriptions that can be used to develop more effective systems by utilizing techniques such as attention on the description level. For instance, we can train the system to pay more attention to descriptions containing the main subject's name when describing a picture of that individual. By doing so, we can increase the likelihood that the system will accurately describe the subject in question. Moreover, we can utilize the description categories to assess the system's performance from the user's perspective, which we cannot accomplish through traditional evaluation methods. For example, we can determine the percentage of descriptions the system correctly identifies as containing the main subject's name. If the system's performance on this task is low, it may indicate that the system is not paying attention to the right parts of the image. Therefore, we should consider the description guidelines' limitations and the system's performance on descriptive tasks alike when evaluating and developing image description systems. If we consider the gap between current systems and the desired descriptions as valuable knowledge, we can utilize it to guide the development of more effective attention mechanisms on the description level. We can achieve this by incorporating a description category layer into the mechanism, which we can further optimize using a novel criterion

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more likely to hold rigid views, we observed increased dissemination of misinformation. These findings suggest that the spread of online misinformation is influenced by offline cultural patterns. We also discovered that misinformation spread is lower in areas with higher levels of education, whereas the impact of population size depends on the level of civic engagement in each state. We propose a framework explaining the interplay between geographic culture, personality traits, economic conditions, and the spread of online misinformation. We evaluated this framework using data from 48 contiguous US states, ultimately contributing to the understanding of online misinformation spread as a complex issue rooted in local characteristics. We also provided reusable code for researching Reddit comments. We propose strategies for reducing online misinformation spread, including promoting civic engagement and conscientious behavior in local communities. We concluded that the spread of online misinformation is a complex issue with deep roots in local culture, rather than being caused by the features of social media platforms. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring ways to incorporate speech patterns into learning algorithms and robot control systems. Experimental data is available for download at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3QOE3T. This work is an initial step towards understanding the auditory aspects of human instruction and it is hoped will spur further interest in exploring the auditory elements of human robot interaction. This study has several applications including developing more efficient learning algorithms, improving speech enabled robotic interfaces, and creating a greater understanding of the importance of audio in human robot interaction. This can be achieved by analyzing speech patterns in various contexts of human robot interaction. This research can be a foundation for developing more advanced learning systems that incorporate multiple modalities of input including speech, that are more efficient and provide better performance than current systems. This knowledge can also be utilized to develop more effective speech enabled robotic interfaces that utilize current technologies such as speech to text systems. This is particularly important for applications in healthcare and education. This research can be a initial step towards a greater understanding of the importance of audio in human robot interaction that goes beyond the scope of this study. This knowledge can be a foundation for further research in areas such as social robot design, human robot collaboration, and robotics education. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose a method for comparing the semantic values of utterances and provide an example of how this approach can be applied to a specific conversational system. Additionally, we present a design for a test driver that automates the process of executing test cases on a real-world conversational system. Notably, our testing framework utilizes existing implementation details of the system, specifically its underlying semantic structure, to facilitate effective testing. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of automated testing techniques for conversational systems, and we invite readers to engage with our proposed ideas and help us refine them through feedback. With the increasing complexity of modern conversational systems, rigorous automated testing is essential to ensure the correctness of their behavior. To achieve this, developers require a testing framework that seamlessly integrates with the underlying structure of these systems, and provides a precise means of specifying desired behavior. Furthermore, comparisons of the semantic values of input commands and system responses are crucial for developing meaningful test cases. To demonstrate the applicability of our proposed approach, we developed a working test driver for the Amazon Alexa, and our results show that compared to a random-based approach, our method yields a substantially lower ratio of system responses that require human intervention (i.e., 'unknown' responses). Concretely, for a test suite consisting of 1,000 prior commands, our approach reduces the number of 'unknown' system responses from 488 to 34, achieving a notable improvement with just 30 additional 'unknown' responses when comparing to an ideal scenario of zero 'unknown' responses. Additionally, our evaluation reveals that the majority of 'unknown' system responses are repeated across consecutive executions of the same command, implying that they are likely due to limitations of the system rather than genuine errors. Thus, our approach is likely to uncover a significant subset of genuine system faults with minimal effort. Notably, our approach is not device-specific

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, our research provides insights into feasible real-world applications and system designs for addressing sparsity in recommender systems. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIBE/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Furthermore, Hypatia's versatility allows it to be used in conjunction with other solver engines via seamless integration with Julia's modeling languages. The resulting data and methodology are thoroughly available for open scrutiny through an accompanying GitHub repository. The proposed approach and the resulting hypatia solver are valued for their potential to significantly enhance the effectiveness of various optimization applications involving exotic cones. The success of these applications is measured through a case study of a real-world problem involving a large-scale supply chain optimization challenge. The proposed method is also related to two previous approaches, one form of the submodularity partition problem and the multi-resolution maximum likelihood estimator. The latter two applications are renowned for their complexity and have historically required substantial computational resources, albeit to different degrees. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, but also stress the importance of reviewing and validating model generalizability on local datasets before deploying such systems broadly. Our results reveal that private EVs can either enhance or decrease the time required for the grid to recover, depending on factors like transportation policies and grid management strategies. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings show that this attractor exhibits sensitivity to changes in the parameters that govern the agents' motivations, ultimately leading to the loss of the pattern's organization and a shift from a fixed point to a random, disorganized state of motion. Additionally, our research reveals that this attractor's dynamic state can be classified as a chaotic system, as demonstrated by the presence of a characteristic fractal known as the Mandelbrot set, which shares the same geometric structure. Through this research, we also introduce a novel interpretation of the Mandelbrot set's cultural significance, reframing it as a symbol representing the complex interplay of autonomous decision-making and chaos, rather than a manifestation of a mathematical property. We conclude by highlighting the potential applications of this research in understanding complex social dynamics and identifying patterns in biological systems. This research is an extension of our previous study published in the journal Chaos, and through a greater focus on theoretical analysis, we have made significant improvements to our initial numerical findings. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our data reveal that the electronic and magnetic properties remain stable across the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, suggesting that rare-earth element substitutions are viable, enabling the creation of stable multifunctional materials. Finally, our study predicts the interplanar distances and the energies of electronic states in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series with precision. Experimental verification of the predicted band structure and the effect of Cm content on the electronic and magnetic properties are suggested for future research. Theoretical calculations of the thermoelectric properties, the Seeback coefficient, the figure-of-merit, and the electronic and thermal conductivities are also presented for all materials under study. The results demonstrate the possibility of designing rare-earth based spintronic and thermoelectric materials through element substitution, thereby opening up new avenues of research in this field. The data presented in this paper have been embedded in the Materials Express Database under the heading GdSn3-CmSn3 or with individual compound designations such as CmSn3 or GdSn3. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts the mass range of these composite particles to be around 0.5-10 TeV, and assumes that the vacuum energy density is very close to zero. The bilepton model is distinguishable from other extensions of the standard model, like the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, due to its predictability of low mass range for particles beyond the standard model. The paper also discusses the possible connection between the bilepton model and the value of the Higgs boson mass. The possible connection between the bilepton model and the value of the Higgs boson mass remains the paper's sole speculative element. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Ultimately, our investigation reveals that the standard ordered generating sequences comprise a permutable group within which the Coxeter length and standard length coincide, thus confirming a conjecture proposed by R. Shwartz. Additionally, our findings specifically show that the element corresponding to a subset S of {1,2,...,n} can be represented as a product of braid generators through standard ordered generating sequences, which further supports a broader conjecture also proposed by R. Shwartz. Our research on the finite classical Coxeter group An yields analogous results, offering a more refined understanding of its underlying structure. Finally, our studies have implications for the Coxeter length on the horizon of the infinite Coxeter group An. Our analysis involves presenting delta-sequences for the group An, which enable us to define the Coxeter length and demonstrate that it shares the same properties as the standard length, thereby demonstrating that the standard length represents the weak distance within the horizon of An. Our research also explores the connection between delta-sequences and the standard ordered generating sequences of An. By utilizing the ordered generating sequences, we demonstrate that the horizon of An can be characterized as the set of elements whose Coxeter length is finite, which among other benefits reveals that the group An possesses a significant property termed solvable complexity. Our investigation of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, An, and Sn includes finding the weak distances of subgroups, demonstrating that the Coxeter length is a strong metric within certain specific subgroups, examining the relationship between Coxeter length and other established metrics, and discovering that the horizon of An comprises a distinct structure when considered with the weak distance metric. Our research on the symmetrized Coxeter braid group Bn(σ) reveals that it exhibits a similar structure to Bn, although it requires a modified standard ordered generating sequences definition

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this approach, we re-examined the Hubble diagram for the SN Ia subset with $z \geq 1$ using Pantheon data and found that the matter density density $\rho_{\rm m}$ could be calculated with a degree of precision that is an order of magnitude greater than previously achieved, albeit with a larger uncertainty of $0.026$ than the one reported using Planck data alone. Nonetheless, the combination of SN Ia data and CMB anisotropy patterns reveals a matter density density $\rho_{\rm m} = 0.040 \pm 0.026$ based on this analysis. Moreover, this research highlights the significance of considering weak lensing effects on SN Ia observations, particularly at higher redshifts, and highlights the value of using existing observational data to inform the halo galaxy mass distribution. Finally, we anticipate that the accuracy of this approach will improve with the introduction of larger SN Ia datasets and more precise galaxy positioning through future sky surveys. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, this demonstration brings the development of practical photospin interfaces in silicon based on T centers into feasibility, leveraging existing industry infrastructure and offering a pathway for further optimization. Furthermore, the elevated frequency of the T center's optical transitions and the coexistence of microwave and optical transitions in the same energy range make these defect centers an attractive choice for threshold-like quantum computing architectures. Ultimately, this research shows that T centers in the 220nm SOI layer can be thought of as a 'quantum silicon layer' with both physical and technological advantages. To emphasize this concept, the name 'Silicon Quantum Tier' was coined to emphasize the distinctive properties of this middle layer, with implications for overlying metal oxide field effect transistors, optical interconnects, and quantum information processing devices. The research presented here is a part of a broader study on the Silicon Quantum Tier, with results on spin-orbit interaction, thermal stability, and the integration of metal oxide field effect transistors with T centers in the lower layer. The advantages of T centers in silicon also need to be coupled with the challenges of scaling the information encodation process, leading to a proposal for a new type of quantum architecture that utilizes graded information encoding. The success of such a scheme was verified through simulation with up to 128 qubits of graded encoding per integrated circuit. The research on the Silicon Quantum Tier has the potential to address quantum computing's significant challenge of scaling production, with a proposed factory design for mid-layer quantum layer fabrication that utilizes 200mm batch process silicon manufacturing, with projected costs per qubit that compare favourably to other proposals for quantum processors. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we outline the potential advancements in treating desensitization treatments as part of learning, rejection treatment, and donor retention, which presents promising areas for future research. Overall, our study provides insights into the strategic decision-making required for kidney transplants with incompatible donors, and the potential complications patients face with these transplants. We advocate for a personalized approach that takes into consideration individual patient requirements and priorities. The study's findings are relevant to healthcare professionals, patients, and organizations responsible for managing kidney transplants, and highlights the value of desensitization treatments, and the importance of developing more effective treatments to increase the likelihood of transplant success. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the word2vec model, highlighting the limitations of these learned embeddings, while also demonstrating the complexity of financial text corpora. Our research tools are available at https://github.com/jiawen95/word2vec-analysis. Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the word2vec model and sheds light on potential future work, such as model development that can capture the diversity of corpora distributions. Our financial text dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jiawen95/finance-sentiment-corpus. Our analysis suggests that the traditional bag-of-words approach, despite its limitations, can be more effective than these learned embeddings in certain polarized domains due to its better ability to distinguish true frequentist synonyms. Our research has implications for the potential disentanglement of these models and highlights the challenge of incorporating external knowledge into these learned embeddings, which could facilitate this disentanglement. Our study also offers a theoretical framework for the evaluation of other learning methods that employ the Skip-gram architecture. Our financial corpus dataset and research code are available for public use, offering a foundation for further research in the analysis

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research and its findings are relevant to a variety of applications, such as learning from observed patterns of competition, discovering optimal treatment strategies in bandit settings, and uncovering stable network configurations in distributed learning. Our approaches have been put through extensive simulations to demonstrate their effectiveness and efficiency in various settings. Our algorithmic innovations, along with the established theory, have been utilized to develop an empirical guide for optimal algorithm parameters in relation to problem variables, further highlighting the scalability and efficiency of our approaches. This research has been physically tested and theoretically proven to be an efficient solution for finding rationalizable equilibria in multiagent learning settings, extending beyond the theoretical boundaries established in previous studies. It has been shown that our approaches are not only environmentally friendly but also yield superior performance compared to the 2021 benchmark, meeting the high standards set by the most challenging game scenarios. Our approaches have been evaluated in realistic simulations of complex multiagent learning scenarios, spanning across various configurations and sizes. It is worth noting that the term "environmentally friendly" is used in this context to convey the polynomial sample complexity of our approaches in relation to the number of players.
