Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a versatile tool called `pdf4lhc` that can amalgamate diverse theoretical predictions of process PDF dependencies, incorporating the effects of web services and precomputed DGLAP kernels with PDFs, and making it accessible for use in grid environments. Although primarily designed to support the development of PDF fitting codes for LHC physics, this tool can be utilized in other hadron collider projects. On the same note, we also introduced a new PDF fitting code called `pdffit5` that leverages the `pdf4lhc` framework, emphasizing flexibility through the use of web services for DGLAP evolution and PDFs, and the possibility of conducting studies at the TeV and beyond by precomputing high-energy DGLAP outputs. It is noteworthy that the DGLAP web service architecture introduced here has implications for web service design in general, emphasizing the importance of component reusability, modular architecture, and standardization. Ultimately, the `pdf4lhc` and `pdffit5` tools are valuable contributions to the PDF fitting and phenomenology communities, and the associated papers are available at [1, 2]. The FCFOM benchmark framework used to evaluate the performance of PDF candidates can be found in [3]. The Standard Model Monte Carlo simulations used to validate the performance of PDF candidates are part of the initiatives described in [4, 5]. The work presented in this paper has been supported by a research grant from Svensk Forskning i Finland (SysMiML) and the Academy of Finland Project Number 294303. The development of the `pdf4lhc` tool was facilitated by discussions with H. Honkela, T. Hahn, and S. Moch, while K. Pondes and V. Vesterinen contributed to testing the tool. The research conducted as part of this project is also published

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. A key advantage of VRED is its flexibility, as it can be integrated with both general and model-specific experience reduction techniques, and its efficacy is illustrated across multiple scenarios. Moreover, the study offers an intuitive assessment of variance-related costs and informs users on how to optimize the trade-off between data efficiency and target distribution estimation. Additionally, the VRED framework provides actionable guidelines for optimizing the underlying policy optimization algorithms as well as the system itself. The study's findings are made publicly available through an interactive online tool to facilitate further exploration. The proposed VRED experience replay method is suitable for various applications, including robotic control, grid exploration, and game-playing agents. The study's results have implications for a wide range of reinforcement learning scenarios involving multiple influencing factors, slow system dynamics, and complex, high-dimensional systems. The underlying VRED framework is comparable in complexity to standard experience replay, making it an appealing solution for addressing the scalability challenges of reinforcement learning. The research demonstrates the VRED framework's versatility, as it can be applied to various systems and algorithms, and offers a foundational understanding of the relationships between variance, data efficiency, and optimal policy discovery. The study's results are a significant step towards developing more efficient reinforcement learning methods that effectively utilize previous experience to optimize complex systems. The research is primely focused on dynamic system optimization through reinforcement learning, but it also has connections to other important topics such as statistical theory, automated design, and complex system management. The study's results highlight the importance of considering the underlying dynamics and data properties when designing the learning process, and it offers a varianced-based perspective on experience that can be applied to other challenging learning scenarios. The study's findings address a key limitation of current reinforcement learning methods and provide a scalable and efficient solution that can be applied to a wide range of applications involving multiple influencing factors, complex systems, and various learning algorithms, by prioritizing the most informative previous observations. The research is underpinned by three novel theoretical contributions

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our solutions leverage sequence-to-sequence 
models with customer-specific texts provided as context, leading to a deeper 
analysis of dialague diversity guided by listener targets. Our code and datasets 
are available for use at https://yamc.ai/multitalk/.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. This package is designed to streamline the process of testing galaxy evolution through simulations of the given type, and is an invaluable resource for investigating the merits of different modified gravity models within the context of large-scale structures. The code is available at https://github.com/RobertsonQuintin/MG-GLAM. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple time multiple SLE with branching (mtmsl\eb) on these domains. This process generates branching boundary segments at points where the time parameter reaches zero, evolving according to a multi-time Karlin-McGregor process. We also derive laws for the scaling limits of mtmsl\eb on the upper half-plane and the orthant, both resulting in the same limit: a process that traces random branching paths in the complex plane, with branches growing according to the Dyson model. This scaling limit can be viewed as a multiple time multiple SLE with branching (\be) on the real line, with a time parameter mapped to the horizontal plane through the Schramm conformal map. This resulting process generates branching boundaries at points where the time parameter reaches zero, leading to a Karlin-McGregor process governing their evolution. This paper also establishes the scaling limit of multiple time multiple SLE with branching on the upper half-plane and the orthant, leading to a new domain branching process, which can be described by solving a system of stochastic partial differential equations. This process, referred to as the $\mathcal{Y}$\eb equation, consists of the Chern-Doob equation and the Karlin-McGregor process. This paper also establishes that the scaling limit of mtmsl\eb on the upper half-plane and the orthant can be characterized by the $\mathcal{Y}$\eb equation, the Karlin-McGregor process, with branches growing according to the Dyson model. This process, referred to as the mtmsl\eb yield process, is a strong solution to the $\mathcal{Y}$\eb equation. This paper also proves the existence and uniqueness of the strong solution to the $\mathcal{Y}$\eb

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. The extension's numerous innovations also tackle longstanding challenges
in software development, such as automating testing, managing dependencies,
and securing collaborative projects, and WorkingWiki's robust framework can be
easily extended via 'plugins' written in common programming languages. Despite
its advanced features, WorkingWiki retains a user-friendly interface and
intuitive documentation, making it an exceptionally accessible and versatile
tool for collaborative software development and scientific publishing. The
WorkingWiki source code is now publicly available on GitHub, where users can
access its features, modify the extension, and contribute to its further
development. The underlying 'WorkingWiki' architecture has been featured in
a presentation at the 2023 Conference of the International Society of

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the application of this model led to the identification of a reaction rate reservoir within the jet flame that resists linear response to acoustic vibrations, causing a delay in reaction rates that contributes to the instability of the jet flame. This phenomenon was demonstrated to be unaffected by the direction of acoustic vibrations applied. Consequently, this study demonstrates that the disintegration of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within jet flames leads to reaction rate oscillations, which in turn contributes to flame instability. This implies that increasing turbulence within jets could be an effective means of mitigating thermoacoustic instability. We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0
u  eta  eta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass would have difficulty detecting a signal. Therefore, while the impact of an extremely light dark matter field on the $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay is novel, it is unlikely to be observable through such experiments. This research also points to the possibility that an extremely light dark matter field could explain the observed intensity of galactic cosmic rays, particularly those with masses exceeding $10^{24}$eV. The condition that allows this scenario to occur is a variable density normalisation of the ultra-light dark matter field, which could be determined through future cosmic ray studies or other experiments involving dark matter. The investigation of the impact of an extremely light dark matter field on various low-energy processes in the early universe is a promising area for future research. The effect of this field on the abundance of baryons during the big bang nucleosynthesis and the formation of the light element helium-4 will both be explored in upcoming studies. The presence of an extremely light dark matter field could also influence the formation of structure in the universe, which will be examined through numerical cosmological simulations. Additionally, the potential connection between this field and quadratic mass terms in the effective Hamiltonian of the standard model, which could result from a particular new physics scenario, will also be considered in subsequent research. The potential of future double beta decay experiments to detect a signal driven by an extremely light dark matter field is limited when searching for an effective mass of less than 10^(-3)eV. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The paper also examines the nonlocal version of the Einstein spacetime hypothesis and determines the solutions for static and rotating axially symmetric gravitational fields. The nonlocal gravity theory's nonliniarization and its relation to the Einstein field equations are also discussed. The paper concludes with an examination of the geodesic deviation equation in nonlocal gravity theory. The result confirms that the nonlocal gravity theory inhibits the gravitational radiation emitted during the collision of two masses, which means the theory is compatible with the Einstein equivalence principle. The paper also uses the nonlocal gravity theory to calculate the magnitude of the nonlocal effect on the de Sitter spacetime's curvature. The result indicates that the nonlocal effect results in a decrease in the de Sitter spacetime's curvature from $48\pi$ to $12\pi$ per unit volume. The volume curvature density of the nonlocal Minkowski spacetime is $-4\pi$ per cubic centimeter. The paper also examines the nonlocal gravity inside a charged massive scalar field cloud around a Kerr-black hole. The result shows that the nonlocal effect delays the onset of instability in the cloud and prevents the cloud from fragmenting. The paper also considers the linear perturbation equations off the Einstein spacetime hypothesis and investigates the nonlocal effects on the emitted gravitational waves' frequencies, amplitudes, and power spectra during the collision of two masses. The result confirms that the nonlocal effect results in a decrease in the maximum frequency of the emitted gravitational waves and increases the amplitude of the waves with certain frequencies. The paper also examines the nonlocal effect on the curvature of the spacetime inside a charged massive scalar field cloud around a Kerr-black hole. The result indicates that the nonlocal effect reduces the curvature of the spacetime in the inner region but increases the curvature in the outer region. The paper also examines the nonlocal effect on the cloud's radius

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel genes associated with microRNA processing, mapping precise mutations associated with a bowel infection and in identifying long-range interaction between a gene and a specific trait-associated SNP. Our approach and results are available at http://genomics.cshl.edu/tracker/. Our study reveals the intricacies of genomic elements' influence on specific traits and provides new insights into genetics. Our approach has been designed as an open framework that allows for the application to a wide range of traits and genomics data. Our detailed analysis of one hundred plus tissues and cell types across different organs and conditions can serve as a foundation for future in-depth explorations. Our data and results are accessible through the following link http://genomics.cshl.edu/tracker/. Our study demonstrates the significance of considering functional genomics in the analysis of genome-wide association studies. Our approach has the capability to enhance the biological understanding of specific traits and can serve as a framework for future genomic investigations. Our results reveal the complex relationship between different genomic elements and various human tissues and cell types. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of recurrence times also diverges from a linear relationship, instead showing a significant slowdown as time goes by. This study's findings, combined with theoretical modeling of mass transfer and evolution, suggest that a significant portion of the Milky Way's neutron star binaries with the lowest masses will remain undiscovered and likely black hole binaries. The actual population of stellar mass black holes in the Milky Way's center is therefore likely to be substantially smaller than previously estimated. The research also offers a theoretical framework for the minimal observable lifetime of a LMXB, relying on the system's evolution and the availability of fuel for mass transfer, and highlights the importance of more sensitive telescopes for detecting more of these variables and improving the understanding of their evolution. The current study is limited to the Milky Way but the same principles apply to other galaxies like the Large Magellanic Cloud. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In both cases, rotation allowed the star to maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning, despite it not being possible if the star were non-rotating. Additionally, we found that instead of experiencing electron capture, some stars could reach the point of shedding mass and shrinking, instead experiencing sustainable hydrogen burning powered by barionic rotation-induced f-mode oscillations, rather than nuclear reactions. This occurrence might happen to stars with initial masses between 0.5 to 0.9 solar masses, experiencing extreme spin caused by binary interaction, and rotating very low-mass stars with initial masses between 0.01 to 0.05 solar masses, experiencing spin-down over time. This research suggests that rotating low-mass stars with sustainable hydrogen burning capabilities might have surface temperatures between 60,000 to 80,000 Kelvin, and could be identified using upcoming all-sky surveys. This implies that such stars might be more common than previously thought, especially in the Magellanic Clouds, a nearby galaxy known for its low star formation activity. This could provide an explanation for the limited occurrence of very low-mass stars in our own Milky Way galaxy. This occurs despite our galaxy having the ideal conditions for the formation of these stars, suggesting that rotation plays a significant role in their development and survival. This research also highlights the importance of considering rotation in the development of sub-stellar objects, especially for those experiencing extreme spin caused by binary interaction, or those rotating very low-mass stars with initial masses between 0.01 to 0.05 solar masses, experiencing spin-down over time. This could lead to the discovery of new populations of very low-mass stars

This model reveals that radiation energy undergoes a transition from a power-law to a linear relationship with time, which can be utilized to determine relevant parameters, such as the initial energy, radiated density, and kinematic factors. Furthermore, this model allows for an in-depth examination of both the luminosity upper limits and the jet breaks, and it is capable of simulating observable phenomena from various angles and distances, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of gamma-ray burst (GBR) radiation dynamics. Additionally, this model can be integrated with other applications, such as the radiated spectra and the polarization of radiation. Moreover, this model has been utilized to develop a novel ranking method for selecting the most energetic GRBs based on radiation energy. Given its versatility, this model can be employed in various astrophysical contexts, including supernovae, quasi-stellar objects, and binary neutron star mergers. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In addition, an algorithm has been created to find the minimum number of nodes necessary to break in order to obtain a planar representation, and this number can serve as a threshold to evaluate the simplicity of Bipartite graph visualizations. In scenarios where the number of nodes to break is unknown, an approach has been developed to incorporate additional input parameters, such as the maximum number of nodes to break and the minimum edge density, into a metric that ranks graphs by their complexity, making it possible to identify the most challenging examples. In the process, a study has been conducted to determine how different aspects of graph structures influence the difficulty of visualizing their representations. Furthermore, a dataset of intricate Bipartite graph examples has been created along with a comprehensive experimental analysis that compares different graph splitting methods, leveraging various performance metrics such as the number of nodes broken, the resulting edge crossings, and the overall simplicity of the representation. In the context of complex Bipartite graphs, a comparison has been made with conventional approaches that split nodes randomly or uniformly, demonstrating the advantages of the proposed method that targets the minimum number of nodes required to yield an edge-free representation. In conclusion, the developed approach has a broad scope of applications in the visualization of Bipartite graphs, representing a significant contribution to the field. The underlying algorithm and proposed metric have been made available through an interactive online tool that can be accessed via a dedicated website. The underlying algorithm and proposed metric have been published in a conference paper titled "Splitting the Task: Easy-to-Visualize Subgraphs of Complex Bipartite Graphs" which has garnered significant interest, sparking discussions on platforms like Reddit and Twitter, and influencing the development of the website. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chen-YuYen/AttackOnFL. Hence, we hope it will contribute significantly to the security and privacy community working in the domain of machine learning. Moreover, potential practitioners and organizations can benefit from it by using it as a guide to prevent possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. We propose several feasible strategies to prevent possible breaches, while highlighting several challenges that arise from several possible implementations. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Notably, our method is found to consistently outperform RFF, often to a significant degree, and also compares favourably to orthogonal random features and the Nyström method in various scenarios. In addition to its scalable kernel approximation capabilities, this method can be configured to efficiently utilize meta-information, thereby enabling the construction of graph-based neural networks that utilize both node attributes and inter-node connections. This is demonstrated through a series of experiments involving multiple graph-based neural network architectures and large datasets. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. If this hypersurface is not compact, we found that it can be mapped to a hypersurface within the space of n+1 dimensions with constant negative curvature -r^2. If this compact hypersurface has a boundary, we determined that its boundary is topologically equivalent to a circle defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. If its boundary is not compact, we found that it can be mapped to a hypersurface within the space of n+1 dimensions with constant negative curvature -r^2. Finally, we also explored and identified relationships between this hypersurface and geodesic loops on its boundary. This research was inspired by a 1979 study by Galloway and Eschrig and a 1981 study by Galloway, and it also builds upon a 2005 paper by Daniel Gounelas. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, threshold values are established to determine when the removal of an individual node leads to the main component breaking into two or more distinct components. Additionally, the average size of the removed component is calculated and analyzed across different network sizes. Interestingly, the findings reveal that above a certain threshold, the average component size remains relatively stable and is directly proportional to the network size. A demonstration of the applicability of these micro-level analyses is provided through a simulation of an attack on a real-world web link network. The results show that the distribution of node removal sizes aligns with a power law, exhibiting the same 3/2 ratio observed in Cayley trees, despite differences in network topology. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated by showing that the average component size obtained through the micro-level analysis matches the outcome of a actual network attack. The power law nature of the distribution of node removal sizes in Cayley trees is attributed to the randomly distributed edges in the network, rather than the presence of scale-free characteristics. To demonstrate this, a scale-free, non-scale-free, and semi-scale-free network model is presented to illustrate the distinct differences in their node removal sizes when applying the same micro-level analysis. The potential applications of the derived formulas in network immunization are discussed, along with the challenges faced in generalizing the findings to more complex networks. The importance of a micro-level analysis of network attacks is highlighted, demonstrating that a deeper examination of individual node removals can provide a more precise understanding of network vulnerability. The paper shows that the application of percolation theory to Cayley trees leads to a precise analysis of network attacks, whereas a similar investigation of more complex networks requires additional specifications of the network structure. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Additionally, this research provides a basis for exploring hybrid gravitational electromagnetic phenomena facilitated by these detectors. A key aspect of the design can be tested using existing gravitational wave detectors, potentially revealing hidden parameters about the detectors' optical properties. The sloshing Sagnac design presents a promising solution for addressing the quantum limitations of signal-recycled detectors and lays the groundwork for investigating hybrid gravitational and electromagnetic phenomena. The idea can be tested using existing gravitational wave detectors, offering insights into their optical properties, and provides a foundation for developing future hybrid detectors that facilitate the detection of gravitational waves entangled with quantum electrodynamical fields. The sensitivity of the detector can be tested in the high-frequency range, where the influence of optical losses becomes significant, and implementing new technologies such as fiber recycling systems or optically linked power and signal recycling configurations is being explored. The development of the sloshing Sagnac design also enables the investigation of quantum effects in detector self-noise, a phenomenon that could provide valuable insights into the phenomenon of quantum gravitation in the context of binary neutron star mergers. The research behind the sloshing Sagnac design has been incorporated into an ongoing study for a third-generation gravitational wave detector in the United States, known as the Ultimate-Scalar gravitational wave detector. This new design can be used in other contexts, such as the generation of entangled photons from the detector itself, or the investigation of quantum entanglement between gravitational waves and electromagnetic fields. The idea of the sloshing Sagnac design has the potential to revolutionize the field of gravitational wave research by opening up new frequencies and possibly enabling the detection of electromagnetic fields that are entangled with gravitational waves. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity. What's more, as MIMO arrays continue to grow in size, the performance of this new scheme improves even further. This work is an extension of an earlier study focused on smaller MIMO arrays and lacking in a detailed algorithm description. A novel hybrid scheduling protocol is proposed to enhance performance in high-density environments with MIMO arrays. With a small-scale MIMO array, the results showed a substantial increase in connected devices, a significant decrease in connectivity delays, and improved overall connectivity. However, with larger MIMO arrays, the performance of the hybrid protocol increased accordingly, demonstrating the positive impact of array size on performance. A similar hybrid protocol was investigated in a simulation with a massive MIMO array, showcasing improved performance with larger arrays, albeit at the cost of increased latency. Another scenario involved multiple user groups with distinct reception areas, leading to a 90 percent decrease in connectivity delays and a 3.8 times increase in connected devices. This was achieved using a simple hybrid protocol with a minimum reception area of 1 meter² and a maximum of 10 seconds latency. When considering the minimum reception area as a group scheduling criterion, the performance gain was observed to increase exponentially with larger arrays, demonstrating the beneficial effect of array size on performance. How the shape of reception areas affects performance was also examined, revealing that areas with a circular shape result in better performance than those with a square shape, due to fewer overlapping areas and more available access points. Consequently, for high-user-density applications, selecting MIMO array shapes that minimize overlapping reception areas is crucial for enhancing performance, along with implementing scheduling algorithms that consider these shapes effectively. This research demonstrates the advantages of large MIMO arrays in crowded settings and highlights the importance of algorithm design that takes into account varying reception areas of nearby devices. A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Additionally, BigApple makes predictions on the minimum mass required for a neutron star, positioned below the lower bound of the estimated value derived from GW190814, which would confirm that its secondary component is a neutron star rather than a low-mass black hole. Furthermore, BigApple allows for the finite temperature neutron star quark-glue anomaly to be re-examined, yielding a critical temperature of 53 MeV for the breaking of symmetry and a value of 2.07 for the quark-glue anomaly density in line with previous research. Finally, the calculated values for tidal coupling constants, canonical f-mode frequency, and the moment of inertia for a neutron star with a mass of 1.35 solar masses and a radius of 30 km are presented, demonstrating the BigApple's capability to describe neutron star oscillations. Overall, BigApple provides a comprehensive theoretical framework that successfully interprets GW190814's data and makes predictable predictions on the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The research also offers a theoretical basis for studying neutron star quark-glue anomaly and tidal forces within compact stars. The effectiveness of BigApple is set to be assessed through future observations, particularly those from LISA and DECIGO, which will have greater sensitivity for detecting canonical f-mode oscillations in neutron stars and the minimum mass required for them to exist. The BigApple platform is designed to be extendable, allowing the addition of new forces and density functionals to improve the accuracy of its predictions. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Despite the advantages of this design, including reduced two-photon entanglement errors and improved resilience to slight mismatches in laser beam intensity ratios, the development of practical applications is limited by the need for lower frequency modulation and the introduction of spontaneous photon emission errors in ion traps. This issue could be mitigated by altering the laser modulation pattern or exchanging standing-wave light entanglement for seeded random entanglement. A proposal is also proposed for implementing Molmer-Sorensen gates with a high degree of frequency robustness on larger chains of ions, involving the synchronization of multiple laser frequencies with a constant offset, and featuring robust entanglement generation across a wide frequency range following initial frequency calibration. This proposal is successfully tested on chains consisting of five to eleven ions. This research demonstrates the implementation of robust Molmer-Sorensen gates on multiple-ion traps, and presents a novel, scalable scheme for efficient, robust entanglement generation in large chains of ions. This new scheme addresses the difficulty of achieving efficient entanglement with multiple-frequency lasers on large chains of ions, and could serve as a building block for large-scale, noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers. This method of robust Molmer-Sorensen gates can be combined with various ion trap types, including fixed traps, segmented traps, and trapped ion crystals in a thermal state, and has been successfully tested on chains consisting of up to eleven ions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Thus, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ is an intriguing example of a correlated Dirac system, offering an exceptional opportunity to explore the interplay between strong interactions and unusual electronic properties. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves competitive results with respect to current state-of-the-art methods on the in-the-wild face alignment datasets AFLW2000-3D and Florence, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling complex face alignment scenarios. The code for our proposed technique is publicly accessible on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/SADRNet/SADRNet.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. The proposed estimator and associated theory can be applied to a broader range of linear models featuring dependent data samples. The current research builds upon and extends existing results in independent settings, notably obtaining risk convergence rates for infinite-dimensional models, evaluating the performance of the ridge estimator, and analyzing the risks of estimator algorithms. The study's primary contributions are three-fold: it introduces a novel approach to estimating the integrated covariance of autocorrelation matrices, provides important implications for estimating dependent processes, and offers a framework for understanding the relationship between data interdependence and estimator risk. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent challenges in addressing this issue, we propose alternative incentive mechanisms that encourage storage units to adopt a more balanced approach, one that strikes a compromise between reducing risk aversion and rewarding them for exploring profitable pricing opportunities. This proposal is tested and evaluated through simulations based on actual market data. Our results suggest that carefully designed incentives can make storage units more resilient to price fluctuations and, in some cases, encourage them to explore opportunities in periods with abnormal price fluctuations. This, in turn, could lead to greater stability in future power grids. This research also raises important questions about the design of incentive schemes and the information storage units require to make informed decisions, and highlights the need for further investigation into the behavior of energy storage systems in real-world settings. This will provide critical knowledge for developing policies and mechanisms that effectively integrate storage units into the electricity markets of the future. This research is a preliminary exploration of this complex issue and more comprehensive studies are necessary for a more in-depth analysis. This work is a initial attempt to examine risk-averse behavior in energy storage systems and propose feasible solutions, and as such, it is necessary to acknowledge the limitations that arise from the challenges of integrating human factors with technological systems. This remains a challenging issue that needs further consideration from multiple perspectives. This research is particularly relevant to markets similar to the Australian electricity market, but its findings and policy implications are also applicable to other contexts, given the universal nature of risk-averse behavior. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds. Finally, models of atmospheres with substantial atmospheric circulation are identified, and the conditions under which they form are established, offering a foundation for understanding the global dynamics of other planets and moons. Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to execute reliable two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors. The investigation also highlights the scope for improving the efficiency of silicon donor spin quantum processors by optimizing the placement of donors. The most favorable positions and orientations of donors in silicon were found to exhibit the strongest exchange interaction, tightly confined electron distributions, and robust coherence in the absence of an electric field. The most critical configuration was found to exhibit an exchange interaction that is twenty times stronger than the noise caused by coupling to the substrate, and feature a coherence time of approximately twice the record for directly controlled qubits. The conditions that lead to reliable two-qubit logic operations are demonstrated in a range of configurations that are achievable with the current technology, and the minimal requirements for implementing reliable two-qubit logic operations with exchange interaction in silicon donors are established. The findings of this research are displayed in an interactive format that donors can utilize to efficiently develop their own silicon-based quantum processors. The most critical aspect of the research is demonstrated through experimental implementation of two-qubit logic operations with exchange interaction in silicon donors. The efficiency of the code was enhanced to address the significant computational demands of efficiently developing a wide range of silicon-based quantum processors. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Moreover, both the magnitude of the resistance and the number of oscillations demonstrated a strong correlation with the magnitude of the magnetic field applied, and a specific resistance value was obtained for zero-magnetic-field conditions. This result is particularly notable given the challenge of measuring resistance in samples with a large energy gap using conventional methods. Furthermore, our findings provide a clear understanding of the spatial distribution of carriers in these samples and the behavior of carrier reservoirs in HgTe quantum wells under a magnetic field. A notable observation from this study is that a specific resistance value can be achieved while maintaining a minimal energy gap, making this approach suitable for use in challenging applications. This research is also relevant to the design of devices utilizing HgTe quantum wells, such as the recently proposed phase-change photodetectors, and offers valuable insights for optimizing the transport properties of these devices. A hypothetical proposal has been developed as part of this study, where a minimal energy gap is maintained while achieving a specific resistance value, and this approach is found to be effective even in extremely small device sizes. This achievement is particularly notable given the inherent challenge of maintaining a large energy gap in extremely small device sizes. A proposed solution to this problem involves using a unique band structure designed through the use of superlattice structures based on HgTe, and this research provides a solid foundation for exploring this idea further. Although the initial investigation focused on HgTe quantum wells, the findings and proposed models are also relevant to other materials that exhibit a similar energy spectrum structure, such as HgCdSe quantum wells. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of Dynamic TDD, despite its difficulties, offering greater flexibility for future cellular networks. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed system demonstrates comparable performance to models trained on larger datasets but with a significant reduction in computational requirements. Ultimately, this paper's approach provides a reliable and efficient solution for enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models in critical settings. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. In the process, we establish a relationship between $J_n^T$ and the colored Jones polynomial of a long, thickened tube, presenting another instance of volume conjecture behavior. In addition, we outline the framework for extending $J_n^T$ to a polynomial colored after several iterations of a construction similar to the one used for the colored Jones polynomial, and speculate that this could be useful in addressing the volume conjecture for links in a thickened tube following a specific geometry. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, the study validates the reliability of developed models, explores potential conflicts of interest, and provides a comprehensive comparison with leading WSD models utilizing publicly available datasets.  The proposed framework and related results have been made available for public scrutiny.  Future research directions and potential extensions to the study are also discussed. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement was used to estimate the total quark-gluon scattering cross-section at the same energy, with a value of 106 nanobarns and a 20-nanobarn uncertainty. These results demonstrate the capability of the CMS experiment to study heavy quark production in heavy-ion collisions and have implied limitations on initial conditions in nuclear matter. Furthermore, the measurement serves as a crucial benchmark for development of Monte Carlo codes used in heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. The approach used in our work utilizes a novel form of a relative Heegaard splitting, along with established results on the minimality of surfaces with specific homotopy properties. The study of the Heegaard splitting type relationships has significant implications for the investigation of the boundary surfaces of certain minimal submanifolds in the context of the Bernstein problem. The research on these topics was facilitated by the investigation of the local heegaardizing properties of maps that are relatively 1-homotopic. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior results than conventional methods, as measured by model performance and parameter robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/zuoyu2016/jkfcv. Moreover, our advice to machine learning practitioners considering our proposed approach is to experiment with varying levels of J and K that are optimized for their specific datasets, as well as to explore other methods that further minimize variance while maintaining reasonable computational costs. In addition, our work proposes a straightforward assessment of model robustness relying on the stability of model performance when tested with different training data configurations, which may serve as a complementary benefit beyond the primary advantage of performance improvement. In the appendix, our study also visualizes the intricate relationships between model performance, parameter tuning and the j-k FCV method in depth. In addition, our research paper is structured in a way that enables practitioner readers to easily replicate the results presented, as outlined in the appendix design outlined in Figure 1. In the section on model performance evaluation, the appendix further delves into the implicit biases present in traditional k-fold CV, as well as the potential risks and possible solutions. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Our work, along with the code and data available at https://github.com/ghaffariam/FABE, provides a viable solution for addressing various computational problems, including constrained optimisation, the most probable explanation, marginalisation, and sampling, by combining the efficiency of finite state automata with the versatility of Bucket Elimination. Our findings are a significant step towards developing more efficient graphical model computation by minimizing the size of the subproblems, which we demonstrate can be accomplished through a variety of underlying automata representations, with the optimal choice depending on the problem at hand. Our approach has far-reaching implications, given the broad range of applications involving the use of underlying structures on subproblems, such as context-free generative models, clustering, and explicit inference. Our evaluation process followed the established guidelines, which involves conducting experiments on a diverse set of problems, switching between 64-bit Linux and Windows, and using the following programming languages: Python 3.9, C++ 17, and Java 11, on machines featuring Intel Xeon and AMD Ryzen 9 processors. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Furthermore, we showed that the shape of the absorption profile can be utilized to measure the velocity distribution of ultracold gases with improved precision. For example, in the case of randomly moving atoms, a certain level of spread in velocity can lead to a complete loss of contrast in Ramsey interferometry due to the reappearance of excited states as a result of momentum redistribution through collisions between the atoms. Our study suggests utilizing the absorption of a short pulse of light at a specific frequency that is resonant with a particular transition in ultracold atoms, instead of the traditional method of utilizing a broad light source and detecting the resulting fluorescence. This approach offers various advantages, including the ability to measure velocity distributions with a precision of one meter per second, and can serve as a precise tool for examining interaction effects as well as incorporating multiple light fields and interactions with ions or molecules.
