When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Overall, this work reveals the intricate relationships between friction, anisotropy, and shear and provides a robust platform for extrapolating experimental data and guiding simulations of this complex nonlinear process. Nonetheless, the fundamental questions surrounding shear jamming remain unresolved, as the absence of a suitable criterion for this state transition leaves it unclear whether it is a distinct phase transition or a continuum of anisotropic points of no return. The anisotropic points of no return are investigated in detail using a new model that accurately captures the dynamics of bi-liquid structures, also known as fish-eye patterns, observed in dense mixtures undergoing high shear stresses. The research reveals that these anisotropic points of no return are characterized by unique fractal geometries and 3D bi-liquid structures that can be fully characterized by a set of universal parameters that include the anisotropy of points of no return, the anisotropy of fracture, the anisotropy of particle alignment, the bridge fraction, the bridge length scale, the bridge radius, and the bridge distribution, all of which can be predicted through the integration of microscale and shear-dependent interactions into the dimensionless variable that defines the distance from shear jamming. The comprehensive framework developed in this work has a wide range of applications, from improving simulations of bi-liquid structures and nonlinear dynamics to informing theories of the shear thickening transition and bi-liquid phase transitions. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, allowing further exploration of its underlying principles. The study of the special Askey-Wilson algebra $A(n)$ reveals it is manageable, with it being shown that $A(n)$ is analogous to $sR(n)$, thereby obtaining its presenting relations. A more general form, known as the $ext{universal}$ special Askey-Wilson algebra, is then introduced, denoted as $uA(n)$. Both the special Askey-Wilson and universal special Askey-Wilson algebras are found to be equivalent to $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, thus both are considered a part of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, offering a different understanding of its underlying structure. The research discussed in the paper also enables the computation of the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of both the special Askey-Wilson and universal special Askey-Wilson algebra series. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made the paired-permutation test exact in the large dataset limit, meaning our algorithm can be used on very large datasets with minimal increased computation cost. We've also introduced a new metric, the effective sample size, to evaluate the efficiency of paired-permutation tests. Finally, we've conducted a series of experiments across eight benchmark NLP tasks and different evaluation metrics, demonstrating the advantages of using exact paired-permutation tests over approximate methods. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a specific kind of veering triangulation, with this characterization being inherently distinct from its underlying topological properties. Furthermore, a method for constructing a veering triangulation from a loom space is outlined, and the implications of this construction on the topology of veering triangulations are explored and compared to their original definitions. Prior to this research, the topological properties of veering triangulations were established solely based on their construction methods, which included both branched coverings and the Reeb graph of their triangulation. Hence, this new understanding establishes that the topology of veering triangulations is, in fact, determined by their underlying loom space topology. Lastly, this research provides the foundation for a more in-depth examination of the relationship between loom spaces, veering triangulations, and fillings of 3D space. It is also noteworthy that this research has implications for the study of pseudo-Anosov flows and surface homeomorphisms, as it reveals that these flows' and homeomorphisms' topological properties can be characterized at a more fundamental level of their underlying loom space topology. It is observed that the loom space for the identity veering triangulation is topologically equivalent to 3D space with its leaves removed and its remaining structure being equivalent to a filling of 3D space. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Ultimately, our findings indicate that at the planned parameters, the cross-section for the process is too small, and more intensive or more sensitive experiments are necessary for detecting the effects of the two leading HEFT coefficients. We also outline potential optimization paths for future experiments. In the latter part of this research, we consider an alternative beyond-Standard Model scenario the Minimal Walking Technicolor (MWT2), and find that the cross-section for the process is significantly smaller in the MWT2 scenario than in the HEFT case, making the search for double Higgs boson production in this process challenging at the two planned colliders. We also outline possible alternative searches for MWT2. This research demonstrates the value of studying double Higgs boson production in the $WW \to HH$ subprocess within EFTs at future colliders, and highlights the importance of incorporating beyond-Standard Model effective theories into the proposed searches and analyses. We emphasize that the primary means of discovering new physics through Higgs boson physics will be the study of anomalous Higgs boson decays in the SMEFT. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Furthermore, our findings also revealed that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow increases with centrality, which we attribute to initial collision configurations more prone to triangular over elliptical geometry in more central collisions. Moreover, by modifying neutron star-radius constraints, we were able to simulate the impact of different radius ranges on heavy ion collisions, and discovered that tighter constraints result in collisions more likely to feature triangular over elliptical geometry. Ultimately, our research suggests that triangular flow may serve as a more sensitive indicator of dense matter radius than elliptical flow. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be viable for both explicit and implicit time-stepping methods, and its effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in this work. The results show that by combining the proposed line search method with appropriate time-stepping techniques and spatial discretization schemes, it is possible to develop efficient numerical methods that balance both accuracy and property preservation. The associated code is available online as the Preservative Numerical Toolbox can be used by the community. The impact of this work is further highlighted by the low computational cost required to ensure property preservation, as demonstrated in the experimental results. The research presented in this paper has significant implications for the numerical solution of various PDEs, including the two-dimensional Euler equations, the Navier-Stokes equations in a rotating sphere, and the three-dimensional Euler equations. The simplicity and efficiency of the proposed line search method make it an attractive option for large-scale numerical simulations involving time-dependent PDEs. The code used in the experiments is part of the Preservative Numerical Toolbox, a free and open-source software available online at https://github.com/PreservativeNumericalToolbox. The research data generated during the experiments are available at https://doi.org/10.26192/329512. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. Furthermore, we present a straightforward approach to incorporate external information, such as intraoperative contrast agent mapping, into the registration process. The resulting navigation data can be utilized for further analytical purposes, such as identifying likely tumor spreads or evaluating surgery outcomes based on postoperative scans. The development of an efficient non-rigid registration algorithm for real-time laparoscopic liver surgery navigation enables a feasible and accurate mapping of pre- and intraoperative data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. We also present the design of a spiking neural network based on random neural networks, along with the proposed 'Sleep-Wake' learning algorithm that enables the network to adapt during classification tasks. This proposed algorithm leverages the benefits of both sleep-based synaptic pruning and a wake-phase neural network to ensure that the network's classification performance is optimized. We provide comprehensive experimental results demonstrating that our spiking neural network delivers consistently better performance when compared to other existing techniques, including traditional artificial neural networks, based on various evaluation metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and mean average absolute percentage error. We also present the results of experiments conducted on real-world hardware, showcasing the energy-efficient performance of our proposed spiking neural network. We have made the proposed model and associated data sets available for public use. We believe that the proposed spiking neural network, coupled with the 'Sleep-Wake' learning algorithm, has the potential to serve as a pioneering example of a randomly generated neural network that can be effectively fine-tuned for wide range of classification tasks, while also providing significant advantages in terms of energy efficiency when deployed on real-world hardware. We propose that this model can be used as a platform for further research and development in the field of spiking neural networks. We also provide practical guidelines for others who may wish to utilize the proposed model in various applications. We have made the code and data sets available at the following repository: https://github.com/ArashPoursvil. We hope that the proposed model and associated data sets will contribute to the advancement of spiking neural networks and related research in the field of artificial neural systems. We are confident that our model can be used as a starting point for other research initiatives and projects, and we look forward to seeing the innovative ways in which it will be utilized by the scientific community. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not a necessary condition for the E2F property by introducing the cube root of a 4-cube, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by a value, to show that there are infinite families of E2F cubic graphs that cannot be classified based on their edge-colourings. Our research also involves finding all infinite families of E2F cubic graphs in the literature, which were previously unknown. Our work lays the groundwork for further investigation into the underlying characteristics of E2F cubic graphs. Our accompanying paper explores the relationship between these graphs and their topological properties. Our research has significant implications for the theory of graph invariants, particularly in relation to the fact that many E2F cubic graphs have the same chromatic polynomial as the cube graph. Our research also highlights the limitations of the Jiang-Zhang conjecture in relation to cubic graphs. Our accompanying paper also delves into the relationship between these graphs and their topological properties, which shares some similarities with the results obtained by Brualdi, Schellenberg, and Vanslangen in the 1980s. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, Timeloops system call learning can be an important resource for future secure containerized applications following microservice architecture. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. Our approach and results contribute a starting point for further research into strategic decision-making in soccer. Our code is available at https://github.com/kevin94012/SoccerReinforce.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, the proposed WRI and ESI methods demonstrate the feasibility of these techniques with real-data examples and the need for further research into challenges related to large-scale solvers.  In addition, a potential advantage of WRI over ESI is also highlighted, involving the preservation of the physical wave equation accuracy.  In the context of non-linear inversion, this property could be valuable to ensure that the generated model at each iteration still satisfies the wave equation, and to prevent the inversion from being diverted from the local minimum area preserved in the WRI formulation.  In other words, the preserved wave equation accuracy in WRI could serve as a type of regularizer to prevent the inversion from being trapped in local minima.  In the context of linearized inversion, this property is obvious as the zero-order linearization of the wave equation still holds, and this property was actually leveraged in the proposed thesis to develop the WRI formulation by treating the extended source as the model perturbation.  In this context, the robustness of the WRI formulation to the choice of the regularizer is also demonstrated, along with the preserved property of using the number of sources as the regularizer.  In addition, the challenge of the storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations is also a major challenge in the context of ESI, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. Finally, some limitations are identified in the current formulation to prioritize simplicity over generality. Two possible extensions are presented that could address these limitations, although they are not a part of this research. 

One possible extension involves enabling the decision-making approach to generate a corresponding Turing machine for a computable function, in addition to determining if the function is computable. This machine would have a specific property called the "prefix-computation property" that is previously undefined. To facilitate this extension, new rules are proposed that characterize the property in question, and it is demonstrated that if a function is computable, then it is possible to generate such a machine efficiently, requiring only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, in contrast to the more general $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement mentioned earlier. 

The other possible extension involves examining the relationship between the original model of two-way transducers and a more accurate equivalent model that consists of two separate components: a Turing machine with a specific property and a source that filters regular languages. This source filter component can be efficiently decided using a more general rule that preserves regular languages under a specific operation, an achievement that was previously unknown. This achievement demonstrates that the source filter component itself can be reliably determined to be continuous, if the underlying Turing machine is considered continuous, using only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methods used here provide a framework for investigating the animacy spectrum across different species and in different cultures. The VTC animacy database is also presented as a publicly accessible resource. The research and database underlying this study have been used in recent work on the cultural influence of VTC animacy representations and the neurobiological foundations of agency perception. The study's findings and methodology offer implications for future studies on the computational models of VTC animacy representations and the neural mechanisms of social agency perception. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. This motivation underscores the need for accurate and versatile modeling tools that can effectively capture the complexities of a super-spreader scenario. The result we derive also highlights the fundamental challenge of determining the effective $R_0$ value in such scenarios, where the effective value may change significantly over time following the super-spreader event. The explicit expressions we obtained for the effective $R_0$ value may be useful in informing strategies for mitigating the spread of a disease during a super-spreader event, particularly in settings where accurate $R_0$ values are crucial for guiding critical public health decisions. The proposed model assumes that the duration of interaction between individuals is significantly shorter than the overall epidemic period, which allows the application of a simplified approach to modeling transmission dynamics. This assumption holds true in many real-world scenarios involving the transmission of respiratory pathogens, such as during conferences, festivals, and other mass gathering events. The resulting model, which includes the effective $R_0$ value as well as expressions derived from the assumption of independent interactions between individuals, aligns with findings from existing studies on super-spreader events. The model can be further developed to account for factors such as the limited accessibility of certain areas and different transmission probabilities among different population groups. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The proposed correction technique is available for the community to use, and further optimization strategies are suggested for future development, including integrating fill fraction evolution equations into inversion codes and conducting more comprehensive testing of algorithms and techniques using simulated data sets. The current study contributes to the understanding and solution of the Bperp bias problem but also highlights the need for more complex simulations that better reflect real-world scenarios, such as incorporating turbulent plasma dynamics, non-uniform noise, and 180deg field component ambiguity resolution, as well as exploring optimization algorithms and regularization methods as part of the inversion process. The research focuses on observations from solar convective zones but the findings and proposed solutions are generally applicable to the measurement of magnetic fields in other stars. The study's approach and findings are intended to advance the development of inversion codes and suggest new testing methods, and it provides a framework for evaluating the performance of inversion algorithms and code versions, which is critical for achieving consistent and accurate results. The paper presents a detailed analysis of variance (DAV) calculations, a novel metric that assesses the performance of inversion algorithms and code versions by comparing the differences between directly inverted data and smoothed target data sets. This comparison is a objective indicator of the bias and variance of inversion algorithms

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our demonstration includes a solid state physics example - the Heisenberg chain - as well as a classical physics example - a simple field theory model - both exhibiting severe sign problems when sampled at high filling levels. By achieving a speed-up of several orders of magnitude for small-system tests, we are able to extend the integration path to the full filling level without any artificial limitations. Our results are further validated by accurate comparison with exact diagonalization data. Our architecture has broader implications for solving other complex many-body problems characterized by sign problems or similar challenges. Our code is available at https://github.com/QMtower/SignProblemMC. Our research focuses on a specific sign problem, but our approach is a general-purpose neural network solver for various Monte Carlo sign problems. Our proposed method can be used as a key component within more complex neural network architectures. Our research demonstrates linear scaling of the determinant cost, an improvement over existing methods that achieve comparable performance at a higher cost. Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy. Moreover, we establish that the currents resulting from the action on the boundary of a group via its automorphisms have zero entropy if the automorphism isn't an inner automorphism, whereas the associated boundary action's currents have positive entropy if the automorphism isn't the identity. Additionally, we establish an connection between currents, topological entropy, and the growth of a group, demonstrating that a group G has linear growth if and only if the current representing the action of G on the boundary of G has zero entropy. Finally, we show that non-zero, positive topological entropy can be associated with the free group's currents, allowing for its calculation using a variant of its full group at infinity's complexity. This variant, denoted as ɣ_n(F_N), is determined by the growth rates of its subgroups, and as such, it directly relates to the topology of the full group at infinity rather than just its asymptotic convergence properties. Consequently, while the current representing the free group F_N has zero entropy, its associated ɣ_n(F_N) enables the distinction between different topologies on the full group at infinity F_∞. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.  ReCross's simplicity, efficiency, and excellent performance make it a compelling choice for unlocking the full potential of massive language models across various tasks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that massive language models are capable of valuing new information based on its relevance to their internal representations, and that ReCross succeeds in capitalizing on this inherent property to enhance their cross-task generalization. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Furthermore, we establish connections between the boolean complex and existing literature on subspaces of reflections in Coxeter groups, also exploring properties of these spaces. Specifically, for the symmetric group S_n, we find the homotopy type of its boolean complex is equivalent to a collection of (n-1)-dimensional spheres, with the number of spheres given by the (n-1)th Catalan number, also recoverable from a distinct formula presented in a related work. Additionally, we establish that the boolean complex's homotopy type is analogous to a known result involving the Lascoux-Schutzenberger bump complex, with a calculated example provided for S_4. Lastly, we introduce the term "strongly decomposable" to characterize Coxeter groups, including finite groups and those whose underlying set has a specific dimension, also exploring related properties and connections to the boolean complex. In the process, we establish rules for combining Coxeter groups, also examining the resulting homotopy types. Ultimately, our investigation paves the way for future research into the boolean complex in more general settings. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Finally, we conducted an policy-based experiment utilizing the peaking coefficient as an evaluation metric, and our proposed model demonstrated superior performance in comparing with traditional machine learning models and current natural language processing techniques. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we propose novel algorithms that dynamically update the loss function in response to input data, building on the principle of hypernetworks. Through comprehensive testing on six distinct image classification datasets, our results demonstrate substantial performance enhancements, supported by descriptive analytics of network weight evolution. Finally, our approach is versatile and easily adaptable to other supervised learning problems. Our project is hosted at https://loss-learning.org/. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our proposed dataset and associated algorithms are designed to address the widespread existence of logical errors in models, particularly in scenarios requiring the inference of events from known facts.  Our efforts are a initial step in creating a comprehensive framework for everyday reasoning based on causality and effects.  Our code and dataset are available at https://atomicdataset.org/.  Our proposed dataset has a significant range of applications in artificial intelligence, including but not limited to integrative learning, graph-based learning, and reinforcement learning, by providing a foundation of intuitive causal relationships that can be easily understood by humans.  These causal connections can be challenging to capture using only machine learning algorithms, however with the right design, they can be learned from vast amounts of unstructured text based on the underlying structure of conditionality.  Our proposed dataset provides a framework of actions, thoughts, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions, which are all key components of causality and effects.  Our research shows that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel as evaluated by both human and automated tests following the application of rigorous quality control measures.  Our proposed learning algorithm leverages the conditional structure of the dataset to guide the generation of new knowledge by targeting novel events that arise from combining previously learned patterns of causality and effects.  Our algorithm employs a novel approach to integrate the generative model with the knowledge base by utilizing the conditionality of the relationships to prioritize the integration of new features that result from the combination of existing ones.  Our algorithmic approach is designed to create a model of artificial intelligence that captures the causality and effects of everyday reasoning through the deployment of robust quality control measures

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. NISQ-HHL's compact design allows for seamless integration with existing hybrid HHL frameworks, thereby facilitating the seamless transition to Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware for a wide range of applications. Experimental outcomes on real hardware demonstrate NISQ-HHL's efficiency, showing that QCRLL2, a hybrid HHL execution of a random circuit rehearsal, can be accurately performed with just 32 actual qubits. Moreover, the research reveals that for portfolio optimization, it's possible to increase the number of qubits from 32 to 64 by trading off the number of qubits for reduced simulation duration, thereby increasing the number of qubits by 50% with no additional expense. This can be achieved using current trapped-ion hardware, paving the way for the development of actual applications. The NISQ-HHL code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/QuantumSmartAlpha/NISQ-HHL. The research outcomes are accessible on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.00853. The code and outcomes can be utilized by financial institutions, alongside providers of Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware and software, to accelerate the development of actual-world portfolio-optimization projects utilizing HHL on real hardware. The research receives funding from the Australian Government through the Australian Research Council (ARC) as part of the Future Fellow

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. This method allows us to apply existing research on asymptotic independence and sum/magnitude limit theorems for random walks. This approach also enables the derivation of precise distance metrics required for our asymptotic independence result. The sum/magnitude theorems are similar to those obtained by Goldstein and Rogers for simple random walks, although with some differences in the underlying assumptions. The findings of this work can be applied to a recent sampling algorithm proposed by Diaconis and Hicks. The theorems on limit distances can be applied to establish the asymptotic efficiency of their algorithm, thereby answering a question posed by Lovasz. The efficiency of the algorithm, however, also requires the addition of an additional asymptotic independence result for two distinct sets of randomly generated parking distributions. The distinction between these two sets is defined by a Hamming distance metric. This latter result is achieved through an extension of the previous research on conditional random walks by the current author, which involves the application of an independent mechanism to ensure that the random walk is reversible with respect to a specific uniform probability distribution. The extension of the previous research also requires the addition of a new threshold function for the Hamming distance metric, which can be considered as a naturally asymptotically vanishing function. The development of this new threshold function involves the use of the weak law of large numbers for the Hamming distance metric itself. The Hamming distance metric law, in turn, can be derived from the application of the total variation distance law to the probability distributions over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The prospect of utilizing quantum phase slips in nanowires for threshold-based logic applications is discussed. The research presented here is a part of a larger study on superconducting nanowires, one that also explores quantum phase slip switches and tunable inductors. The findings reported here demonstrate the feasibility of adjusting the dc conduction threshold of nanowires by applied voltage, pressure, or temperature, and reveal a notable discrepancy between measured and theoretical capacitive coupling, the latter being much smaller. The mechanism of quantum phase slip is known to be sensitive to surface impurities, as demonstrated by comparing the thresholds of nanowires with and without additional material on their surfaces. The adjustment of the threshold by applied voltage or pressure, along with the observation of the zero-voltage junction potential, the magnitude of Kapitza resistance, and the relation between resistance and applied voltage, are also examined and reported. The research on individual nanowires reveals a wide range of capabilities and limitations, allowing for the selection of suitable materials for specific device applications. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In order to facilitate integration with existing research on this topic, we also present results in a format compatible with existing 'well mixed' models, revealing that the error in underestimating transmission risk can be substantial, with estimates suggesting that up to twenty-fold more aerosol particles may remain in the air than previously assumed, depending on specific conditions. Consequently, we propose that a more accurate'minimum' model is necessary to reflect the true dynamics of aerosol transport in these environments. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrates the value of using detailed airflow models to inform data analysis and interpretation in the context of airborne transmission research. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of distinguishing between different models of aerosol transport to ensure a thorough understanding of the complex factors involved in the spread of airborne pathogens. To facilitate replication and expansion upon our research, we have made both the raw data and the code used to generate the results openly available. As for future work, we suggest exploring similar scenarios with different confined configurations and examining the value of more sophisticated airflow models when transmission risk is the primary focus of study. In addition, we propose investigating the effective ventilation strategies that emerge from these detailed airflow analyses, with the aim of applying this knowledge to improve public health guidelines. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, a model based on the elastic scattering hypothesis successfully explains the magnetic anisotropy and Hall effect behaviors in the multilayer layers, by incorporating interfacial cobalt layers with precise control over thickness. Notably, the largest Anomotous Hall Resisitivity was observed in a 1.5 nanometer thick Cobalt layer, and it showed a resistivity of 0.84 millimillien per square when considering the skew-scattering mechanism alone. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that elastic scattering of free carriers by sites at the interface can lead to the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers, and it also uncovers a higher-than-expected Anomotous Hall Resisitivity in the smallest Cobalt layers. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope that the methodology and findings presented here will contribute to the understanding of neural network training with a limited Lipschitz constant. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Despite being specifically designed for ditau events, this code can be modified to simulate other rare processes involving the collision of protons at the LHC. For instance, it can be used to evaluate the resonant production of the $\mathrm{Z}\gamma$ system, which could lead to the discovery of vector leptoquarks in future experiments. As for the code itself, it is an open-source, public contribution to the community of particle physicists using vector leptoquarks in their research. This code is an improvement over previous versions, featuring improved precision and a more sophisticated algorithm to enhance efficiency. Furthermore, it includes accurate corrections to the production of ditau pairs via the exchange of gluons, which is a significant improvement over existing codes but can be disabled in certain scenarios. This code has been tested in various scenarios, including those involving the collision of heavy quarks and the collision of protons at the Tevatron particle accelerator, in addition to the LHC. As a result, it is a reliable code for evaluating precision corrections to the production of rare processes involving the collision of protons at the Tevatron and the LHC. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. Nonetheless, the study concludes that the primary driver of connections within the text is the relationship between successive statements themselves, with the underlying ideas of CT remaining essential for understanding the coherence of conversations. Moreover, the study suggests that the revised CT can be used to improve the systems' ability to recognize connections within the text. Ultimately, the study contributes to the understanding of how computer systems that recognize connections within a text function, as well as the limitations of CT in this context, and presents a feasible way to enhance the systems' performance. The research raises important questions about the relationship between coherence in conversations and the connections between successive statements, and provides a feasible approach to improving computer systems that recognize these connections. The study's findings have implications for the development of computer systems that identify relationships within a text, and could be applied to various applications, such as developing better conversational agents. The study's methodology, which involves developing and evaluating a specific metric in a controlled environment, as well as the use of a search-based method to analyze the computer systems' performance, provide valuable insights for future research in computational linguistics. The study's results demonstrate a clear connection between the systems' ability to recognize connections within a text and their ability to model the coherence of the text itself, and reveal that the systems' performance is influenced by their tendency to favor more recent statements, among other aspects. The study's approach, which involves developing a metric to evaluate the systems' performance in a controlled environment and analyzing the text itself using various elements, offers a valuable framework

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The most effective model obtained displayed a 307% improvement in accuracy when compared to the traditional Euclidean distance approach, thus providing a meaningful improvement in geospatial distance estimation for WiFi fingerprinting. The research concluded with an exploratory analysis of potential applications of this approach to large-scale commercial datasets that remain anonymous due to contractual agreements. Ultimately, this research is anticipated to contribute to the development of accurate indoor positioning systems across various settings, including those mentioned above, as well as in healthcare, sports, and entertainment industries. The corresponding machine learning model becomes part of the IndoLoc open-source framework, a widely applicable framework for indoor geopositioning mentioned earlier. The framework, in addition to the model, incorporates an automatic WiFi fingerprinting data collection framework, as well as various existing algorithms and approaches to indoor positioning, thus offering a comprehensive resource for the indoor positioning community. The code for this research is available at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/IndoLocProject/IndoLocFramework/. The corresponding paper for this research was presented at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) in a work titled "A Scalable Approach to Indoor Geometry Inference using Machine Learning over WiFi Fingerprinting". The paper can be accessed through the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08502. The related dataset for this research is available at the following link: https://doi.org/10.79140/SN/202

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this research provides a theoretical framework for integrating beam-RF interaction into multi-beam, multi-pass energy recovery linac simulations, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of stable beam filling patterns in various scenarios. Ultimately, finding the optimal filling pattern in these scenarios can increase the maximum beam current by 2-4 factors or more, offering significant benefits for future energy recovery linacs. This study's findings are demonstrated through simulation results of a proposed 500 MHz, 1.2 GeV energy recovery linac. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. By contrast, under the NMRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV resists such decomposition, thereby demonstrating a more intricate structure that must be accounted for in BFKL equation extensions to NNLL accuracy. In such a scenario, the usual approach of using a leading colour approximation is no longer valid, and a more comprehensive understanding of two-gluon CEVs is necessary to achieve NNLL accuracy in BFKL predictions. In addition, the derived two-gluon CEV can be applied to the analysis of rapidity gaps in hadron collisions beyond traditional LL accuracy, thereby incorporating effects of six-gluon corrections on jet jet production and photon photon processes at the LHC.
