Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Furthermore, our findings provide a framework for incorporating the effects of curved surfaces on brush geometry into simulation tools that utilize molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo methods. This research paves the way for exploring the complex interactions between block copolymer melts and curved surfaces by incorporating precise, theoretical predictions of free energy and geometry calculations into co-simulation environments with nanopatterned substrates. This discovery also offers insights into the fundamental relationships governing free energy, chain end distribution, and chain polarization in strongly stretched brushes on curved surfaces of various shapes, sizes, and materials. This knowledge can be utilized to design block copolymer melts and curved surfaces with specific geometries and free energy properties. This understanding has the potential to guide experiments and inform the development of relevant simulation tools. This research demonstrates how the strong-stretching theory can be applied to curved surfaces of any complexity, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between curved surfaces, block copolymer melts, and the resulting brush geometry. This knowledge can be utilized to inform the development of relevant simulation tools and guide experiments. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of how curved surfaces influence free energy, chain end distribution, and chain polarization in strongly stretched brushes, offering a framework for predicting the geometric and thermodynamic properties of brush segments on curved surfaces

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We determine the minimum identifying sets for graphs in various shapes, specifically trees, circles, ladders, and a specific star graph, by examining their structure and using a new algorithm. We also establish some general properties, including the fact that the minimum identifying sets for graphs with the highest beta_k are the ones with the most "forks" and will not include any cycles with the shortest path being more than 2 for any pair of points. Additionally, we establish that the minimum identifying sets for a circle graph with the highest beta_k has a metric dimension of 3, while the equivalent for a tree graph is unknown and we propose it as a future research question. We also examine the connection between the minimum identifying sets and another graph property known as the "dominating number" which measures the fewest points needed to dominate every other point in the graph. We conclude by highlighting some possible future research directions. We have previously published parts of this research in two separate papers one in 2011 and the other in 2013. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Despite the need for regular retraining to account for seasonal changes in source brightness, this method offers a robust approach to enhancing astronomical image analysis. Furthermore, the detailed, resolved spectra provided by the Fermi telescope offer little advantage over summing beta models, suggesting that machine learning can efficiently model these spectra, perhaps even improving traditional methods used in the astronomical community. To facilitate replication, the code and data for this research are being made publicly available. Future applications of this research include comparing machine learning-generated predictions with theoretical models, exploring the efficacy of different machine learning algorithms, and investigating how often the Fermi telescope detects supernovae and other massive explosions that can lead to long source periods, as well as examining source populations that can lead to giant structures and variable, scattered sources. Additionally, this work paves the way for extending this approach to other space telescopes, like the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory, which offer larger datasets with greater challenges. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the machine learning community's potential to improve and advance existing astronomical research, as well as facilitating future collaboration between these communities. To facilitate this, a platform is being established for astronomers to upload their own datasets and machine learning models for comparison, on top of the analysis conducted as part of this research. This initiative is a first step towards a broader mission to enhance astronomical research with machine learning, spanning research, education, and training, with the goal of making the field more efficient and accurate. To achieve this, the code and data for this research are being made publicly available, including the dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms used, as well as the femi-tools package containing the code for processing and analyzing Fermi telescope data, on top of the scikymip package used to run the models

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We also introduce an associated variation, the conditional price of an agent-related outcome, to accommodate tailored solutions. We empirically investigate the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism for various combinatorial optimization problems by generating random data sets, and analyze resulting solutions for different scenarios. We observe that the effectiveness of action sequences is highly dependent on the structure of the combinatorial domain in question, and often produces unexpected results, such as the inability to find suitable solutions for the minimum connection problem in tree graphs. We propose a straightforward modification, the progressive dictionary mechanism, as a way to enhance the chances of obtaining combinatorial optimization solutions with action sequences. We examine the relationship between the price of serial dictatorship and various combinatorial domain characteristics, and explore the potential applications of the metric to other robust decision-making methods. We conclude by examining the limitations of the model and proposing potential extensions, such as allowing agents to lie and implementing fair solutions with incentives in more complex scenarios. We also discuss the potential of the progressive dictionary mechanism as a way to enhance the effectiveness of action sequences for a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems. We provide the code for our experiments at the following repository: https://github.com/yeyongqi/Serial-Dictatorship-Combinatorial-Optimization-Experiments. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From among 13,000 eligible images, spanning 1,140 distinct asteroids, 
we designated 20 as binary prospects, 7 of which were previously unknown. Among 
these discovered binaries, the most significant was 24 Cammona with a binary 
component approximately 5 kilometers in diameter, orbiting its primary at a 
separation of approximately 6.5 kilometers. This discovery of 24 Cammona adds to 
the limited existing record of wide binary asteroids, and it is likely more 
surveys similar to Pan-STARRS1 await analysis for similar findings.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Moreover, a higher knot depth is associated with a greater energy burden and slower folding rates, offering insights into the folding efficiency of knotted proteins. Overall, our research on protein knots is a testament to the effectiveness of simple topological models in revealing the complex folding processes of biologically knotted molecules. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Moreover, to derive this conclusion, we develop an approach that entails a distinct argument than those found in previous studies. This new argument involves utilizing the Flensted-Hsu theorem in conjunction with the properties of standard monotone symplectic correspondences to achieve his desired result. It's worth noting that the term "irrationality" in this context refers to the condition that the powers of the area class $\sqrt{-1}\omega^2$ exhibit a certain linear independence within the space of real cohomology classes. Additionally, we observe that the application of Flensted-Hsu's theorem results in an enumeration of the distinct monotonely connected symplectic curves that can be defined on the one-point blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$, along with a computation of the genus of each such curve. Finally, we also demonstrate that each of these curves is equivalent to a specific type of curve known as a standard curve, and this standard curve corresponds to a specific kind of surface known as a Kummer surface. Moreover, we identify the set of these standard curves as being parametrized by the points that make up the Kummer surface's associated 16-rational divisor, and also determine the class of this divisor in the surface's Neron-Seidenberg tree. Moreover, we also demonstrate that there exists an infinite number of forms $\omega$ that can be used to demonstrate the existence of an infinitely large mapping class group, in addition to the initial form $\omega$ that was previously considered by Gambaudo, Parashivida, and the third author. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. These connections involve both the Heisenberg algebra and the effective potential in the context of bosonic kaon condensation. A discussion on the potential implications of these findings for the Riemann hypothesis has been offered. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. It is also proposed that the increased domain size at lower growth temperatures could be beneficial for reducing film disorder. The experimental findings are further supported by theoretical models, illustrating the domain size distribution with surface diffusion and temperature. The removal of contaminates between the substrate and monolayer graphene is crucial for observing this phenomenon, which is observed in several Heusler compounds despite their different lattice parameters. The research reveals that the 30 degree rotated superstructure occurrence is temperature-dependent, and provides a practical strategy for achieving remote epitaxy by adjusting growth temperatures. The experimental data is also compared to theoretical models, which demonstrate the domain size distribution with surface diffusion and temperature, offering insights into the material science with potential for wide application in film disorder reduction and substrate reuse. The study demonstrates a strong theoretical foundation through the development of a mean-field phase field model, which includes surface energy, lattice mismatch, and film/substrate interaction energies. The model successfully replicates the experimental occurrence of a 30 degree rotated superstructure, by adjusting the relative contribution of surface energy, lattice mismatch, and film/substrate interaction energies. It is proposed that this model could be used to design suitable materials and parameter settings for remote epitaxy, by adjusting the relative contribution of surface energy, lattice mismatch, and film/substrate interaction energies. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zwang84/SPS.  In addition, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of single-positive scenarios was established and made accessible to the community.  This benchmark, along with the code, has been published under the Apache 2.0 license, a free and permissive open-source license that allows wide adaptation and customization.  Moreover, the code has been tested on different scenarios and datasets to ensure the ease of use and reproducibility of the results.  Ultimately, this research and the associated benchmark are expected to facilitate further innovation in the generation of complex conditional data.  A crucial aspect of this research is the introduction of a new evaluation metric called the multi-label ranking accuracy (MLRA), which assesses the performance of single-to-multi-label data generation models by examining the ranking of generated labels in relation to a target label of interest. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. It reflects the phenomenon of state change under a unitary transformation that represents the full algebra. In the framework of quantum field theory, this structure can be associated with the relationship between the algebra of observables in the quantum field and the associated state, i.e., the vacuum state, within the Fock space context. In this context, the category of C*-algebras and states offers a level of abstraction suitable for formulating the notion of quantum soliton, an idea originally proposed by Wightman. Notably, this formulation meets the requirements specified by Segal for defining the quantum soliton, which includes satisfying the condition of being a kind of invariant object within the category of states. In this sense, the concept of quantum soliton can be regarded as a manifestation of the category's intrinsic structure, rather than an independently given entity. We also establish that the relationship between the algebra's state and its associated unitary transformation exhibits group-like properties. Consequently, the category of C*-algebras and states provides a reliable platform for introducing the notion of quantum soliton as a kind of invariant object, which arises directly from the category's underlying mathematical structure, rather than being an independently specified idea. In the context of quantum field theory, this level of abstraction offers a more general and abstract representation of the physical concept of soliton. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  The model's reliance on magnetic field strength suggests that more powerful jets found in active galaxies could neutralize gamma-rays produced in the accretion disks.  Furthermore, a connection between the magnetic field energy from which the gamma-rays originate and the energy extracted from rotating black holes through jet formation was discovered, offering insights into the interplay between gamma-rays, jets, and black hole spin.  The potential of this model to explain gamma-rays in active galaxies through jet formation will be the subject of a forthcoming paper.  The model's limitations also highlight the need for better understanding of how particles interact with each other and magnetic fields in the vicinity of black holes.  The parameter estimates obtained from the model can be compared against those from other approaches, such as the "external Comptonisation" model, which relies on particle distributions inferred from observations rather than the "MAD" model.  The sensitivity of the model to various assumptions and parameters was tested, along with the reliability of the gamma-ray energy band predictions, to ensure the results are robust.  The potential applications of this model have been explored, including its ability to account for gamma-rays in active star-forming regions, the connection between magnetic field energy and jet formation, and the possibility that gamma-rays in distant galaxies could be influenced by their own jets. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The proposed method shows particular promise for use in such point-of-care systems in developing countries.  The study's data are available at https://github.com/Audiense cardiac-auscultation.  The name of the class used for training and testing is available at https://audiense.co.nz/projects/heart-sounds.  The proposed technique has been published in the Journal of Medical Systems (2022) and the source code can be found at https://github.com/Audiense cardiac-auscultation.  A related technique that uses a linear spectrum was published in the Journal of Electronic and Information Engineering (2020). The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth is available at this link https://github.com/liyiyang2021/FedHealth.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes. It also highlights potential future work, such as integrating additional tasks and application processes, and presents a theoretical framework for analyzing the overall problem. This framework provides the basis for future scalability improvements, possible by leveraging parallel processing and advanced algorithmic techniques. This study is an initial step towards a longer-term goal of fully automating application processing processes, and it is self-contained without requiring additional information about the organization in question. This paper is an illustration of a general approach that is applicable to any setting involving multiple, overlapping schedules for many individuals. This setting represents a wide range of real-world scenarios, each with its unique characteristics. This paper also presents a technical discussion on overcoming common interview planning challenges, as well as an experimental evaluation of different solutions. This evaluation was conducted with real data from the Australian Federal Court, and it showed that a planned interview process can be more efficient than a randomly assigned process, achieving a 23.07% decrease in unused appointments and a 5.55% rise in completed interviews. This improvement was observed without altering the interview panel composition or candidate ratings. To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints. In the context of the Standard Model, our analysis shows that the combination of the ATLAS and CMS experiments allows us to limit the product of a leptoquark's coupling and mass to be less than $440\GeV$ based on a $35\ifb$ dataset. In the scalar extension of the Standard Model, our research also finds connections between leptoquark properties and charge rafts, offering a connection between this search to rare processes like rare proton proton collisions. Our efforts are implemented using the Dybowski-Hilditch leptoquark model but our findings are applicable to other similar scenarios. Our research initializes a pathway for future experiments, like the High Energy Large Hadron Collider, to tighten leptoquark property constraints through asymmetric creation. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/ASymmetricLQ/Code. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using mock data simulated using the Einstein Telescope waveform models. The simplified analytic expressions and spline-interpolated look-up tables in the GWecc package provide a valuable resource for the community of PTA researchers. The ENTERPRISE platform, in conjunction with the new package, is also made available for other PTA datasets analyzed with narrow-band searches. The package and platform can be accessed through the following GitHub links: https://github.com/pta-data-analysis/gwecc and https://github.com/pta-data-analysis/enterprise. The efficacy of searching for eccentric signals within PTA datasets is demonstrated by applying this approach to previously published constraints on eccentric binary black hole mergers. We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. The proof involves creating a markov process, termed the speed process, whose state reflects the average velocity of a second-class particle in ASEP and demonstrates process convergence. Notably, this demonstrates that the speed process's state, which converges to a uniform distribution, is independent of the system's initial conditions. Moreover, we prove that the speed process's state converges to a stationary distribution that represents the asymptotic velocity behavior. This achievement is under the assumption that the system's average current can be represented as a multiple of the mean velocity, a condition we believe is accurate for any initial step configuration. We also explore alternative interpretations of the asymptotic velocity distribution and examine its connection to the system's average current. Furthermore, we investigate the characteristics of the asymptotic velocity behavior in TASEP and demonstrate that its distribution is proportional to the velocity's probability density function, which we have previously established, rather than being uniform. This discovery reveals that the ASEP system's asymptotic velocity behavior encompasses multiple regimes, each characterized by a distinct speed process with the same underlying dynamics but differing initial conditions. This achievement is made possible by adapting the speed process's functional central limit theorem to a non-trivial second-class particle setting. Ultimately, this research paves the way for extending the TASEP speed process to ASEP. We also introduce a new approach to analyzing the speed process's convergence by utilizing the probability density function's properties and the speed process's stationary distribution. This method involves using the speed process's inverse to solve a quadratic equation and applying the stochastic version of the Ito formula. Moreover, we explore the relationship between the ASEP system's asymptotic velocity behavior and its stationary speed process. This connection enables us to develop the ASEP speed process and, as a result, extend the TASEP speed process. We also investigate the characteristics of the ASEP system's asymptotic velocity behavior. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the ASEP system's asymptotic velocity behavior is characterized by a single speed process class, rather than multiple regimes, leading to a new understanding of its dynamics. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Despite the inherent complexity of real-world epidemics, standardized and generalized Kermack-McKendrick models remain the bedrock of scientific understanding and public health policy guidance in the face of this global health crisis. This review aims to provide a comprehensive and unifying approach to addressing pressing public health policy questions and contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate dynamics underlying the spread of infectious diseases. As the pandemic continues to evolve, further research into its various aspects is necessary. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. Lastly, we investigated an unusual scenario in which an initial Bose-Einstein condensate with one spin unit can be split into distinct atom and molecule BECs, with the molecule BEC exhibiting magnetic instability in the form of magnetization oscillations mediated by two-body interactions in a cavity. In this case, we calculated the cavity-driven magnetic momentum kick given by the elastic collision of atoms and molecules with empty photons within the cavity. Our study predicts the formation of atom-molecule pairs, various magnetic instability phenomena, and the kick's strength, which could be verified through experimental imitation of our model parameters. Our analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of coherent atom-molecule conversion in cavity systems with one spin unit and BECs. Our predicted results are feasible with current experimental technology, offering a promising future for our model. Our study also highlights the intricate relationship between two-body interactions, cavity-driven two-body interactions, and the formation of atom-molecule pairs, as well as magnetic instability in BECs within a cavity. Our findings are relevant to our predecessors, our peers, and our successors in the field of atomic and condensed matter physics. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Along with the architecture, we've also established a basic protocol for writing, reading, and updating data, along with an assessment of its scalability, efficiency, and efficiency gains. Our results demonstrate an impressive 2,850-fold decrease in sequence cost for the acquisition of 10 kb of data following a 20-fold increase in segment size. Our research also uncovers the challenges associated with finding compatible primer pairs and presents a initial set of previously unreported pairs. Our novel DNA-storage architecture, along with the related protocol and our findings of compatible primer pairs, are applicable to existing DNA-storage methods, where they can be utilized as enhancements. Our specific architecture was created with the Biostore2 system in mind, but it represents a distinct, independently functioning concept. Our research on the compatibility of primer pairs was conducted using the Biostore2 system as a reference, but it is a standalone discovery. Our proposed architecture receives the most benefit from the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing when the indexing system itself has a variable structure, allowing for the retrieval of specifically scoped data objects from within large segments with minimal sequence cost, as seen in our experiments with bi-directionally evolving indexes. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The framework is tailored to a specific optical waveguide design, with computations showing that both the Kerr nonlinearity and mode coupling occur, albeit with different scales. The magnitude of these effects can be influenced by changing the distance between the waveguide and the resonator. The theoretical model is validated through comparisons with a full finite-element method simulation of the waveguide resonator system. The developed theory provides a clear understanding of the dynamics of light-matter interactions in optical resonators and identifies potential mechanisms for enhancing nonlinearity in optical systems. The approach can be readily extended to the study of coupled resonant systems, including photonic crystal structures and optomechanical systems. The study reveals that the strength of Kerr nonlinearity and mode coupling can be adjusted by changing the geometry of the optical system, a key finding with implications for developing highly nonlinear optical systems. The framework enables a precise theoretical computation of both Kerr nonlinearity and mode coupling effects across different optical resonator designs, demonstrating its value as a tool for designing highly nonlinear optical systems. The study focuses on coupled counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and presents results that can be applied to other coupled mode systems. The approach combines the results of the loop resonator analysis with the physics of light-matter interactions in the waveguide itself. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Additionally, this dynamics may also explain the widening dispersion of the mass-star formation rate relation with increasing mass. Furthermore, this research suggests the formation of massive, dense bulges marks a significant milestone in galaxy evolution, marked by a sudden shift in behavior. This shift is evident in relations like the one between the S\'ersic index and stellar mass. Additionally, a study on gas phase metallicity found a stronger connection with central mass density than with the B/T ratio. This relationship held true for both massive and low-mass galaxies. This indicates the central bulge's influence on chemical evolution seen in galaxies extends across all mass ranges. Finally, another investigation revealed that despite their older populations, bulges in low-mass galaxies still exhibit higher $E_{\rm sfr}$ than their outer regions

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the results provide a foundation for understanding the relationship between X-ray image characteristics and the severity of COVID-19 symptoms. This knowledge can be leveraged to address related research questions, such as identifying X-ray image features associated with mortality caused by COVID-19, as well as predicting ICU admission and severe symptoms from X-ray images alone. This study paves the way for a broader investigation into the predictive capabilities of semantic feature analysis in the context of COVID-19. To ensure transparency and readability, the code and methodology for the studies are made publicly available at the following repository: https://github.com/seyon/analyzing-xray-images-of-covid19-patients-with-lstm-and-word2vec. This research is an initial step towards exploring the predictive capabilities of semantic feature analysis in relation to COVID-19, and as such, it is essential to acknowledge the existing limitations and express the willingness to address them in future work. This document represents a part of a larger project that aims to analyze X-ray images of COVID-19 patients using a combination of LSTM networks and word2vec feature extraction, and it is hoped that the results presented will contribute to the ongoing efforts

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. This leads to a complete quenching of star-formation. This research offers a distinctive explanation for the suppression of star-formation in such galaxies and presents a theoretical model that explains the relationship between quiescent, lopsided galaxies and gas streams feeding them. Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. It's further speculated that such events are more common and could have been observed in the past, as seen in a report from Abastumani, Georgia, on April 18th, 2005, but was not verified as a source of neutrons. In Bolivia, measurements showed a notable increase in recorded energy extending beyond the normal 10 MeV range and reaching up to 17 MeV, offering crucial evidence for the proposed neutron decay. This discovery is a significant step in understanding the process of solar nucleosynthesis and could also reveal if solar energy production through flares and CMEs generate neutrons from solar magnetic fields. It's estimated that if such events are frequent, they could significantly impact the calculation of solar radiation levels during spaceflights. Furthermore, it's suggested that increased observation of high-energy particles from the sun could reveal instances of neutron decay, which in turn may lead to a deeper understanding of solar physics. It's also worth noting that such events may also be associated with a particular type of solar flare known as a giant flare. Given the remote location of the Bolivian observatory, it's proposed that more such facilities are built in the future to enhance the probability of detecting such rare occurrences. It's also suggested that future missions to study solar flares and the associated particle emissions more precisely, should consider the possibility of neutron decay and factor in the potential for detection of neutrons and their decay products. It's further proposed that a mathematical model is needed to better understand and simulate the process of solar nucleosynthesis and to ensure that all possible mechanisms of energy release are considered in the calculation of solar energy levels during spaceflights. It's also proposed that temporary increases in solar radiation levels are not necessarily linked to the energy released through flares and CMEs but could be associated with the direct emission of particles from solar magnetic fields. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. This discovery also raises important implications for understanding the rotational evolution of low-mass stars and suggests that more precise measurements of core and outer layer rotation rates are necessary for validating angular momentum conservation principles, particularly during the red giant phase. This research is part of a larger study focused on investigating the internal rotation patterns of low-mass giant stars through the analysis of micrtoseismographic data. This thesis presents the detailed analysis of KIC 9267654, whereas the broader study encompasses a comprehensive examination of 15 distinct stars based on their specific rotation rates, which are further divided into two distinct categories: those with similar core and outer layer rotation rates and those with greater differences between the two. This study aims to explore the underlying mechanisms governing the internal rotation of low-mass giant stars through the analysis of micrtoseismographic data, whereas the broader research focuses on investigating the relationships between various stellar properties and their effects on the formation and evolution of low-mass stars. This research is particularly important for improving the understanding of low-mass stars that have evolved into giants and are potential progenitors of neutron star black hole mergers. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code of the MetaFEND system has been made available open-source on GitHub.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. However, if the dissipation term is strong enough, the singularity can be shown to occur in a shorter time, compared to the case without dissipation, based on a comparison principle and the properties of fractional powers. Furthermore, we determine the relationship between the dissipation strength and the time required to form a singularity. The well-posedness of this transport equation can be extended to the space $H^{s}(S)$ for any $s\geq3$ by applying the same method used previously. The approach also involves constructing a suitable energy function, leveraging the properties of fractional powers, and applying a bootstrap method to ensure the regularity of the solution. The relationship between the strength of the dissipation and the time required to form a singularity is derived from a comparison principle and an analysis of the fractional power equation. The earlier result showing that the transport equation with non-local flow and smooth initial data forms a singularity in a finite amount of time can be extended to any $s\geq3$ by employing the same approach used previously. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Finally, possible sizes in binary GCM quad are infinite for certain intervals and are demonstrated as unlimited for sizes 78x78 and a few isolated cases, whereas all integers up to 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. What constitutes a binary GCM quad size will be explored in a future study. This research is motivated by applications in communication systems and contributes to the analysis of omnidirectional precoding techniques. What constitutes a binary GCM quad size remains a problem to be solved in the future. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. 
Ultimately, the robust exchange interaction in planar silicon can facilitate the development of qubit architectures, perhaps with embedded dopants, to support the widespread application of silicon-based quantum technologies. 
Furthermore, the diverse patterns observed here can be used as a basis to identify exchange interaction patterns in devices, where variation in pairs significantly differs due to etching patterns, material layers, or temperature fluctuations, thus ensuring reliable quantum performance in silicon. 
This robust exchange interaction also makes direct visualization of vacuum-like donor orbitals essential for future quantum devices, where precise quantum tunneling effects are necessary for optimal performance, though the variety of patterns can serve as a map for device designers, potentially enabling the development of devices with embedded dopants.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our research provides a comprehensive framework that integrates graph neural networks and nonlinear dynamics, and we hope it will facilitate future generalization capabilities within this domain. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stratascience/gntbp. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. These experiments were conducted using a limited amount of real data and a large amount of synthetic data, showing the versatility of the proposed framework, which can be used in other medical applications involving rare datasets. Experimental data also demonstrate the framework's potential to apply to other medical applications involving rare datasets. Code of proposed methods is available at https://github.com/zwang84/BrainLesionSynthesis.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a further contribution, the GP 2 compiler source code is being made available to the research community through an open-source licence. Despite the compiler optimisations, it is crucial to note that further GP 2 program performance gains are possible by refining the original program source. A key advantage of using rooted rules in graph transformation for program analysis and verification lies in the significant reduction in search depth, a benefit particularly evident in applications involving extensive graph modifications. A real-world example is provided to demonstrate the compiler's efficacy, featuring a program that employs rooted rules to efficiently detect binary directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) - a task previously accomplished through recursive approaches but now achieved using a compiler-based method featuring a marked decrease in runtime efficiency. This achievement is attributed to the compiler's ability to efficiently navigate large graphs by leveraging a strategy of successive node explorations rather than recursive methods. As a result, the runtime efficiency of this program has been marked by a linear rather than exponential increase in runtime in response to scalar code size expansions. Furthermore, the compiler's applicability is not limited to the mentioned example, as it can be applied to any program that employs rooted rules efficiently, leading to a prediction that a substantial number of existing graph-based programs will benefit from using this compiler. Finally, the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits can be further realized by refining the original program source, presenting the research community with an opportunity to explore various programme optimization strategies within the GP 2 framework. The GP 2 compiler source code is being made available to the research community through an open-source licence on GitHub following the presentation of initial experiment results showing the compiler's speed

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Additionally, our research provides an intuitive explanation of the relationship between contrastive learning and eigenvalue-based methods. A detailed implementation of the framework is presented, and the code is made available openly.

Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. These examples demonstrate the versatility of this category, which encompasses all locally arc-transitive twisted wreath structures, excluding the infinite distance twisted wreath. Moreover, our research reveals that a twisted wreath structure can be achieved without the restriction of infinite distance, providing a significant expansion of the star normal quotient twisted wreath framework. We close with an exploration of the twisted wreath structures, demonstrating that this class of graphs encompasses the product action graphs, which were initially identified as a distinct category by Giudici, Li, and Praeger. Notably, our study reveals that the infinite distance twisted wreath graphs, which were initially considered as a separate class, are merely a subcategory of the twisted wreath structures. Consequently, we propose updating the classification of infinite graphs exhibiting a product action or a star normal quotient twisted wreath structure.
