Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Furthermore, the proposed method is simple and intuitive, with easily interpreted results. The algorithm, called GLAS, is an open-source contribution available at https://github.com/ourpaper/GLAS. The corresponding MATLAB code can be found in the repository with the dataset and examples of use. The proposed GLAS algorithm provides a versatile solution for model selection and sparse modeling, especially when dealing with categorical data, and offers significant improvements over existing methods. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Our approach provides a straightforward strategy for integrating structured information into unsupervised LLM training, and our results suggest that LLMs are capable of accurately interpreting the structure of knowledge graphs. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Furthermore, an analysis of model efficiency revealed that dual-path modules and RNN components can be further optimized by replacing them with more efficient convolution-based architectures. To facilitate widespread use, the DPCRN model has been made publicly available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zhanglei58/DPCRN. In addition, model weights for the Convolution Recurrent Networks component can be found on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zhanglei58/CRN. Moreover, the code and model weights have been successfully tested on recent speech separation challenges, and the underlying research has been presented at the 2022 ACM Multimedia Asia Conference. The work has also been published in the ACM Transactions on Multimedia, Volume 24, Issue 1 in 2022. The advantage of using dual-path RNN models for modeling lengthy sequences in the time domain has been demonstrated, and efficient convolution-based architectures that replace RNN components with dual-path modules have been validated. The feasibility of using these models for modeling sequences in the frequency domain, such as the narrowband condition of the DNS challenge, has also been explored. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. We also introduce a measure to assess the accessibility of multipartite entanglement for novel combinations of systems that are already known to be entangled. This research demonstrates that JC-interactions can be used to generate intricate entanglement patterns, thereby expanding the possibilities for quantum applications. Our findings are applicable to various physical setups, including optical and superconducting systems. Our approach to assessing multipartite entanglement can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, including those involving three to twenty-five qubits. Our data also shows that reducing decoherence in experiments can significantly enhance the quantity of accessible multipartite entanglement. This knowledge can be utilized to enhance the efficacy of quantum devices that leverage JC-interactions for multipartite entanglement generation. Our research spans models involving one to twenty-five qubits, and our results are applicable to various physical systems that incorporate JC-interactions, including those with optical, solid-state, and chemical compounds as key components. Our entertainment value lies in predicting novel patterns of entanglement for various species of atoms and molecules, offering opportunities for quantum simulation in existing experimental setups. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a method to obtain the Wigner function from the optical tomogram by utilizing a Gaussian reference state, and this method is illustrated using a generated Bell-state and an arbitrary coherent state. Ultimately, our research shows that optical tomography, despite the complexity of continuous-variable state reconstruction, can serve as an essential tool for investigating non-classical behavior in microwave systems. Our work also paves the way for developing a database of optical tomograms of various quantum systems, which can facilitate ongoing efforts in state reconstruction and serve as a benchmark for such efforts. This initiative is represented by the optTomBase, a proposed online database of optical tomograms of different quantum states of light. This proposed database is envisioned as a platform for comparing, manipulating, and sharing optical tomographic data of various quantum systems and scenarios, including both theoretical and experimental implementations. This will empower researchers to compare and contrast the optical tomographic patterns of different quantum systems and implementations, potentially revealing distinct patterns of optical tomograms that are robust across multiple state reconstruction methods. This proposed database also has the potential to demonstrate the practical applicability of state-independent, machine learning-based approaches for predicting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of a light state. This involves executing a machine learning algorithm on a miniature sample of optical tomographic data, comprising randomly selected points from the 2D grid representing the state of light, and evaluating the performance of this algorithm by executing the machine learning model on the full optical tomogram of the same state. Ultimately, our research and the proposed database are crucial for enhancing our understanding of the relationship between the optical tomogram and the Wigner function of a light state, thereby facilitating the efficient investigation of non-classical behavior in ongoing and future experiments with both classical and quantum systems. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. Additionally, we derive and decouple the Hamiltonian dynamics associated with these surfaces, which are crucial in the study of molecular dynamics. Ultimately, our research enables the creation of efficient algorithms for molecular dynamics simulations on a broad range of surfaces. To demonstrate the breadth of our approach, we present results for various surface types, including anisotropic, curved, and polyhedral surfaces. Furthermore, our work can be extended to incorporate moments of higher order than those currently considered. By solely focusing on the physical properties of surfaces rather than the specifics of the Hamiltonian dynamics, our approach also offers a promising direction for developing more general surface decoupling theories. We anticipate that our methodology will serve as a preliminary framework for developing decoupling theories on other complex surfaces. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. Our approach, easily integrable with existing RL frameworks, presents a straightforward and efficient solution to enhance NMT using reinforcement learning. We've made the code and models available for public use at https://github.com/Qianhui Liu/RL-NMT Few Shot Learning. Nonetheless, our technique requires less data than the standard approach, our experiments showing that with 200 k tokens, our model sees a significant decline in effectiveness, while with 10 million tokens, the decline is much more moderate. Our approach's effectiveness can be observed across multiple language pairs, including low-resource languages such as Spanish-Arabic and Chinese-Japanese. Our research also compares our action similarity learning approach to alternative unsupervised methods including noise-contrastive estimation and deep domain confusion, finding that our technique yields better outcomes, as validated by metrics including BLEU scores and human assessment. Our approach's efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated by our experiments, showing that our model requires roughly half the amount of data compared to the standard approach, while achieving translation accuracy comparable to the current state-of-the-art NMT using reinforcement learning, as validated by experiments using the IWSLT 2017 English-to-Japanese translation dataset, comprising 200 k tokens. Our research presents a pioneering investigation into the effects of action space size on translation performance in NMT using reinforcement learning, leading to several key findings. We've further explored methods of reducing the action space's size, beginning with the most straightforward approach of vocabulary size reduction, before experimenting with more sophisticated techniques such as dynamic action selection, learning the learner, and teacher learning. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also observed that the energy flux variations followed the expected pattern of a Rayleigh distribution, with the shape being more symmetrical than seen in older records, and we believe this is also likely the result of the plasma fluctuations being less significant at the closer distance. Additionally, we found the solar wind energy distributions were independent of the electron temperature and proved to be non-kurtotic, whereas they typically become more kurtotic as you move closer to the Earth. We also calculated the solar wind particle fluxes, which ranged from 2.5 to 5.5 particles per square meter per second, depending on the approach, and we found these remained relatively consistent across the four approaches, but we plan to investigate this further in the future. The accurate measurements we obtained will be valuable for informing models of the solar wind behavior and the formation of solar winds from the solar surface, as these are significantly influenced by the interactions with solar magnetic fields and plasma fluctuations, which become less random at closer distances. The reliable data we collected will also be beneficial for testing these models and understanding the global structure and dynamics of the solar atmosphere. The unique data set we have enables us to explore additional interesting phenomena observed during the approaches, including unusual regions of altered electron temperature and pressure near the inner edge of the heliosphere, but these are complex and will be the subject of future research. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Additionally, both models show a very narrow, extremely hot layer with a sudden and infinite temperature at the shock wave's front. This layer's width, however, remains roughly one order of magnitude smaller than the distance between the shock wave and the edge where the density suddenly increases. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. A real-world application example is also presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. A key finding revealed is that the algorithm yields solutions that are relatively close to the optimal solution, with the precision adjustable based on communication and malicious activity limits. A notable aspect of this approach is that system parameters do not need to be known in advance, rather they are learned during the optimization process by reliable agents. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes example use cases, such as investigating the impact of instrumental systematic effects on temperature and polarisation maps derived from simulated raw data, and demonstrating the integration of the package with a larger simulator of cosmic microwave background experiments, the'sims_valdes' package. This is particularly important for predicting the effectiveness of future experiments in measuring the optical polarisation of the cosmic microwave background in the multipole space. The package's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stevenspelt/s4cmb, and the project's website is at https://s4cmb.readthedocs.io/. The package's documentation can be found at https://s4cmb.github.io/s4cmb/. The underlying simulator'sims_valdes' is described in a related paper by Spelt et al. (2023) [1]. The research presented here has been conducted as part of the cosmology program at the Max-Planck Institute for Astrophysics, and is part of the Simons Atlas project led by B. Reichardt. The package has been tested on workstations running Linux. The package's source code is compatible with version 3.9 of the Python interpreter. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The proposed MD-CSDNetwork exhibits a significant reduction in computational requirements while maintaining the accuracy of costly, domain-specific models, offering a valuable solution for real-world deepfake detection applications. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/HengtaiZheng/MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of obtaining the embedding of these spaces with angle functions into Euclidean spaces, thereby expanding upon the existing knowledge in this area. 

In the case of uniform spaces, it is demonstrated that the embedding of these spaces with angle functions into Euclidean spaces can be accomplished in such a manner that it preserves the angle function itself. Additionally, this article establishes a connection between the concept of spaces with angle functions and the idea of convex sets within the context of Euclidean spaces. Ultimately, it further elaborates on the properties of these spaces with angle functions, highlighting their similarity to the characteristics of convex sets in Euclidean spaces. 

An area of significant interest in mathematics, the topic of embedding spaces with angle functions into Euclidean spaces has far-reaching applications, as evidenced by the notable results achieved thus far. Nonetheless, this article reveals that there are specific constraints governing the possible embeddings of these spaces with angle functions into Euclidean spaces, thereby highlighting the significance of distinguishing between different types of embeddings. In mathematics, distinguishing between different types of embeddings is a fundamental concept with significant implications, as seen in the example of polynomial embedding spaces with angle functions. In conclusion, this article presents a comprehensive framework for addressing the problems and areas of research related to the topics of spaces with angle functions and polynomial embedding spaces with angle functions. In particular, it addresses the problems initially posed by Menger in 1930, expanding upon the existing knowledge in this area and providing a promising foundation for future mathematical research.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. We also discover connections between the ratios of successive minima and the number of embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$, exploring a relationship called the "volume discipline". Additionally, we investigate the distribution of ratios of minima, demonstrating convergence to $1$ for certain subsets of orders, thereby generalizing an result initially proven for Galois fields by Diaconis and Shah. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the ratios of minima and the field's Galois action, demonstrating that the distribution of ratios of minima is accurately described by a random process called the "volume scramble". This "volume scramble" process, which we introduced in a previous work, originates from a natural, field-specific, random dynamic, and the associated ratio distribution offers an interpretive framework for understanding the dynamic. Moreover, it is evident that the distribution of ratios of minima identifies the underlying Galois action, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for Lenstra's conjecture. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our findings to conjectures related to the distribution of minima in quadratic fields and negative discriminants. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our investigation provides a detailed breakdown of the Forsage network, enables the calculation of transaction fees, and showcases the arbitrary provider rankings as a result of the fixed compensation structure. Ultimately, our research on Forsage, a rare visible pyramid scheme, serves as a unique opportunity to explore the inner workings of these typically hidden scams. Our study reveals the intricate mechanisms of Forsage, a scheme that has been successful in maintaining high participation levels and significant revenues in recent years, despite being a classic example of a scheme that ultimately leads to financial losses for the vast majority of its users. Our research on Forsage also offers a significant contribution to the broader academic community studying decentralized systems, blockchain technology, and smart contracts, by presenting a distinctive application of graph-based analytical methods, contract reverse engineering, and transaction fee analysis, in environments known as "decentralized applications". Our research on Forsage is now available as a pre-print on arXiv, along with the code and data used for the study. Our team is open to collaboration opportunities and invites researchers to build upon this study. In addition, our team is willing to engage with regulatory bodies, as well as providing the research to relevant authorities. Our study on Forsage can be downloaded from the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01749. All code and data are available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/blockchain-skeptics/analysis_of_forsage. Our team also created an interactive Forsage scheme explorer that can be accessed at the following address: https://forsage

We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. This code has the unique advantage of being an accurate representation of the holographic HaPPY pentagon code at a lower, more simplified level of abstraction. It's also worth noting that these tensor networks represent a specific class of haPPY codes - one that includes pentagon-based codes as a subcategory. Finally, these networks can serve as models for understanding the properties of a broad code family - one that encompasses both random haPPY codes and pentagon-based codes, despite differing slightly from these actual code types. These networks have the capability to accurately simulate the behavior of both random haPPY codes and pentagon-based codes by adjusting their parameters. Notably, these networks can also be used to investigate the critical threshold for erasure correction in random haPPY codes. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our process-prediction data is available for public use. 
This research can be viewed at https://www.processmining.org/wiki/index.php/Predicting_Process_Characteristics_With_Deep_Learning.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. As point cloud models continue to evolve with increased precision, our robust validation framework and results will contribute to the secure development of these models.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the impact of dictionary size on representation efficacy provide valuable insights into the design of SparseGAN. To facilitate further research, the code and models for SparseGAN are available openly.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. If the dispersion of star formations is considered, statistical analysis of existing observations shows that the probability of observing interstellar panspermia could be as low as 10 power minus 6. On the other hand, if stars remain isolated, the probability rises significantly, potentially exceeding 10 power minus hundred. Therefore, to increase the chances of discovering interstellar panspermia, it is necessary to examine life-bearing planetary systems in areas where star formations are dense and there is minimal interference from planetary orbits and gravitational forces. If interstellar panspermia does exist, it is anticipated that fossil evidence of microbial life would be found on planets located about 20 to 60 AU from their parent star, rather than extremely distant planets like Alpha Centauri's Proxima b. Moreover, the most probable candidates for these interstellar refugees would be microorganisms capable of withstanding the most severe conditions, such as extreme temperatures, over extended periods. Consequently, searching for life forms that can thrive in harsh environments on planets situated in the appropriate distance from their parent star may hold the key to uncovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. If successful, this discovery could lead to a deeper understanding of the spread of life across the cosmos, as well as the potential risks and benefits for human civilization. Ultimately, the possibility of interstellar panspermia raises fundamental questions about the origins of life on Earth and the need for a re-examination of the assumptions underlying current astronomical observations. If valid, a new dimension would be added to the study of celestial bodies, making the search for life a three-dimensional puzzle. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our study demonstrates the value of integrated analysis of capture and telemetry data, offering a vital framework for future studies involving the joint use of these data types.  Additionally, we propose a user-friendly R package,'sccr', to facilitate the application of these models in future research.  This package provides a suite of capture-recapture and space-based models, including the newly developed models presented in this study.  We also introduce a computational algorithm that incorporates various capture strategies and location information from captures to estimate the models' parameters through maximum likelihood estimation.  The'sccr' package incorporates the algorithm mentioned above and allows for the analysis of capture-recapture data combined with various capture strategies and location information from captures.  As an example, we provide the output of our primary data analysis in the supplementary materials available online.  We also provide a worked example in the package documentation that replicates the results from our study.  Furthermore, we offer a Shiny app to facilitate the package's usage and to provide educational content on the capture-recapture method and related models. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Our approach can be incorporated into a variety of formulations, including optimization problems, by substituting the proposed joint matrix representation. This enables us to explore the stability of multilayer networks in greater detail than previously possible. As an example, we reconstruct the American power grid as a multilayer network and conduct a stability analysis of this complex system. Our results demonstrate that our method can effectively capture the dynamics of multilayer networks, offering a valuable tool for modeling and analyzing real-world systems. Our research on the American power grid multilayer network reveals that the presence of interconnections between geographically distant regions significantly affects the stability of the entire system by influencing the synchronization of local communities. Our findings also reveal that our method aligns with previous research on smaller multilayer networks, showcasing the robustness of this analysis approach. As our largest real-world application, the American power grid multilayer network demonstrates the practical viability of our method, highlighting the value of considering the complex interconnections within dynamic systems that operate across multiple layers. Our approach provides a meaningful reduction of multilayer network dynamics, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics, particularly in regards to the stability of synchronized states. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Consequently, a common misconception among renowned scientists is revealed, and the invariance of the Euler-Lagrange operator is established with a simplified condition. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The design of the algorithm is adaptable to varying delta values and network topologies, including those with narrow degree distribution. The validity of the algorithm is proven statistically through an appropriate test, and the associated parameters are derived with rigorous mathematical analysis, as well as experimental data from real-world examples. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, our results show that this method yields the same physical solutions as the default approach, thus providing a supplementary tool for constructing high-quality initial data. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Moreover, we draw implications for the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials by considering possible mechanisms involving quantum entanglement and spin-orbit coupling. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a substantial anomalous Nernst effect, suggesting that it may be viable for high-energy conversion efficiency applications. Additionally, we outline potential experimental improvements for the anomalous Nernst coefficient measurement. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN, filling a significant knowledge gap in this area. Moreover, our research challenges the previous notion that the anomalous Nernst effect is essentially the same as the anomalous Hall effect in the same material, revealing instead that they behave distinctively in antiferromagnetic materials with non-trivial band structures. While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.

This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the high-level precision of direct cortical recordings in detecting walking-related neural activity and presents a promising solution for seamless interaction with lower limb prosthetics in the future. The findings also highlight the advantages of using ECoG over EEG in this application due to the higher resolution and lower noise levels. To take full advantage of this research, the underlying neural codes underlying gait and other complex movements will need to be fully understood, thereby potentially leading to new insights into the fundamental mechanisms of motor control. The present study also includes a downloadable dataset of raw and processed ECoG recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while walking on a treadmill, presented in the supplementary information. The ecological validity of the results is ensured by recording the data from real-world walking movements rather than simulated ones. The relatively non-invasive nature of the data collection, coupled with the limited distinction between actual and predicted signal components, makes this dataset exceptionally suitable for overfitting detection and training purposes, in particular for the development of real-world BCIs operating on long time scales. The underlying code for the study is also available in the supplementary information and on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/jamesstagg/Long_time_scale_gait_BCI. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdeng/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for various applications such as wildlife monitoring, animal-machine interface systems, and visual prosthetics. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/huseyngul/biolocomotion-detection. The biolocomotion detection framework is viewed as a preliminary step in an object detection pipeline, enabling the detection of biological entities from their movement patterns before their visual appearance is analyzed. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. Empirical evaluation across multiple platforms reveals that NN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including GPU implementations, by a significant margin, especially when operating on extremely large sparse matrices. The Nested Neumann method is a high-performance approximate matrix inversion algorithm that has numerous applications in machine learning, deep neural networks, and scientific computing. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research is further expanded to evaluate the curves' Jacobians, thereby facilitating the computation of fundamental periods and the definition of elliptic regulators. The appendices provide additional mathematical derivations, a discussion on the curves' non-rationality, and an analysis of how the approach can be applied to curves within any genus. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Consequences of the Event Shape Engineering approach on charged hadron and photon production in nuclear collisions are also explored.  Specifically, results show that steeper distribution slopes are observed in events with higher-than-average elliptic flow, while curvature densities of charged particles or transverse momenta remain unaffected.  Also concluded is that cone-like structures of photon pair production are unaffected by event-shape selection, whereas the cross-section for photons paired in a "wrap-around" direction are more likely in events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, suggesting that initial state overtones are capable of influencing two-photon correlations in proton-nucleus collisions.  Finally, findings from the study support recent calculations based on artificial viscosity in hydrodynamics, while also demonstrating compatibility with models incorporating initial state fluctuations composed of distinct harmonic components.  Ultimately, the event shape engineering technique provides a means to precisely identify unique aspects of heavy ion collisions not explainable by conventional fluid dynamics.  Consequently, this approach can be utilized with current and future data sets to delve deeper into the properties of initial state conditions and medium properties in heavy ion collisions.  Furthermore, this technique can be applied in future collisions at the Large Hadron electron Collider, allowing for a thorough examination of the event shape engineering method in proton-nucleus and nuclear-nuclear collisions.  Future research directions for the event shape engineering method in heavy ion physics are also discussed. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our simulation of particle collisions was further validated using high-speed imaging, showing that our algorithm accurately models collision outcomes and shapes compared to experimental data. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, a comparison between the RFT and DEM models of ground reaction forces showed that while the RFT model yielded force predictions with a mean square error of 10 Newtons, the feedback controller successfully compensated for these errors, ensuring accurate height tracking. Ultimately, this research showcases a robust control system that can be hopped to a predetermined height on a dynamically changing, soft terrain modeled by a discrete element method simulation. Hence, this work provides a suitable framework for further investigation into control systems for hopping robots on more complex, deformable environments. It is necessary to note that the current study assumes a one-dimensional model and thus a straightforward up-and-down trajectory, which is a significant limitation given the two-dimensional nature of real-world terrain. Nonetheless, this research paves the way for an expansion of this work to a more intricate and two-dimensional terrain model. It is also worth mentioning that the feedback controller's performance can be enhanced through the use of a state estimator, such as an extended Kalman filter, which would be necessary when moving to a more complex state representation. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The results show that our approach matches the effectiveness of state-of-the-art methods while operating at a significantly larger scale, and it has the added benefit of easily integrable source code for other researchers to build upon. The experimental framework, in turn, has been made open-source and is available on GitHub as well, along with the underlying data for the Wikipedia experiments. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. As such, they demonstrate the practical applications of quench dynamics for enhancing quantum annealing. 

Furthermore, this research reveals that the interconnection between quench and annealing dynamics is influenced heavily by the annealing gap's functional behavior, posing a significant challenge to its accurate modeling, whereas the overall quantum state evolution during annealing remains unaffected by the quench dynamics. Ultimately, models incorporating these findings can serve as a framework for developing quantum annealing algorithms that leverage the underlying connection between quench and annealing dynamics in various Hamiltonian-based optimization problems. As an added aspect, the development of an explicit random Ising Hamiltonian model results in an analytically tractable form of the annealing gap's functional behavior, enabling a direct link with its quantum quench dynamics through non-equilibrium temporal development following the annealing process. This knowledge can be utilized to improve the efficiency of quantum annealing in solving intricate optimization problems by tailoring the annealing protocol to the specific problem dynamics. $d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Thus, the one-band Hubbard model remains a reliable representation for sufficiently
strongly screened layered nickelates, with screening itself being a critical
parameter that significantly affects the ground state and excitations. 
Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of properly screening out
the incorrect components from the original multi-band architecture, which could
be especially crucial for future experimental and theoretical studies of actual
material compounds. 
Lastly, our study involves a generalizable approach that demonstrates the
value of using a realistic two-dimensional band structure description, which
otherwise loses crucial information when reduced to a one-dimensional description. 
With appropriate screening, the one-band physics of infinite layered nickelates
can be accurately captured using a suitable tight-binding array of orbital types,
rather than the commonly used one-dimensional chain or ladder structures. 
Consequently, our work offers a more precise and more generally applicable
framework for the one-band physics approximation in infinite layered nickelates.

As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  The proposed research will enable a deeper understanding of the quark phase's nonperturbative properties and the hadron-quark phase transition's dynamics. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our proof involves an innovative approach, as we have substituted an ancient solution with a recent solution of a specific harmonic equation under certain conditions. This substitution enables us to leverage the recent solution's properties to draw conclusions about the ancient solution. Moreover, we have made significant improvements to the estimate of the space-time $L^2$ norm of the gradient of harmonic functions from 4 to 2, thereby achieving our desired objective. This achievement is made possible by a refined analysis of the relationship between the gradient of a harmonic function and the curvature of the underlying manifold.
