A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. These predictions and simulations demonstrate the material-specific nature of YSR states and Nb's unique properties. Furthermore, theoretical framework predictions for other materials are proposed. Experimental evidence from scanning tunneling spectroscopy for a single Mn adatom and a magnetic dimer made up of two Mn atoms on Nb(110) was used to validate the model. Marginal influence of localized spin polarization on surrounding superconducting material atoms was observed. Moreover, spin-orbit coupling effects were distinguished from exchange field effects. At the same time, necessary extensions to the model are proposed for the investigation of coupled YSR states in antiferromagnetic dimer arrangements. Lastly, the material-specific nature of YSR states and Nb's unique properties have been established. Furthermore, a proposed framework is offered for the prediction of spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities on the surface of a superconducting material by considering the spin-orbit coupling, exchange interaction, and zero-point fluctuations of phonons and spin fluctuations in the material. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  This prediction is supported by theoretical calculations utilizing the Hybrid Functional method.  This research indicates that substituting carbon or nitrogen for titanium would initiate the reduction of Ti4+ and the formation of O2- or O- bonds with the corresponding formation of bondless F or F dimer defects which possess magnetic moments of 4$\mu B$ or 2$\mu B$ respectively.  Conversely, substituting carbon or nitrogen for oxygen would initiate the formation of bondless F or F dimer defects which possess magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ or 4$\mu B$.  This research also demonstrates that substituting N for C in TiO2 would initiate the formation of N-O bonds with oxygen in a NO dimer which could be verified via spectroscopic techniques, and could potentially be a source of magnetism in N-doped TiO2.  This prediction is not observed when substituting C for N.  This research also demonstrates that substituting C or N for Ti would initiate the formation of carbon or nitrogen monolayers at the surface of TiO2.  This research also demonstrates that substituting C or N for Ti would initiate the formation of surface or near-surface states in TiO2 which could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Finally, I show that the elastic process remains too difficult to access with the current detectors, however the semi-elastic process offers a promising pathway to discovering rare top-quark decays and provides the potential to establish stronger limits on these rare processes than currently achievable with other methods. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. Moreover, the degree of polarization can be anticipated to be significant for laser-driven particle sources, given the known robustness of the forward direction emission. The magnitude of the polarization can be anticipated to be even greater when using larger targets due to the deeper interaction of the positrons with the plasma. The degree of polarization may also be modulated by employing a thin solid target composed of a multi-element material, due to the spatial dependence of the electric field in such targets, which could, in turn, affect the position and energy of the emitted positrons. The computational methods employed in this study are feasible for numerous experimental parameters. The efficient simulation codes used meet the memory requirements of high-performance computing facilities for extended simulation durations spanning several seconds. The simulations themselves cover time periods ranging from one to ten optically driven plasma skin depths. The code's ability to handle large numbers of electrons and the inclusion of the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons in the simulations demonstrate the robust nature of the methods. The code's capability to handle large numbers of electrons also demonstrates the feasibility of modeling the interaction between intense lasers and dense targets composed of numerous particles. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that such groups cannot be constructed as infinite, simple groups and that only finite groups like bilateral free groups meet specific criteria derived from polynomial diameter properties. Additionally, it is shown that among finite groups, those with a polynomial diameter are classified into two types: one with a relatively small parameter that does not scale significantly and another with a diameter that scales exponentially prior to polynomially. A significant outcome of this research is achieving an upper limit of polynomial scaling for the diameter of finite groups, which is relevant to outstanding conjectures in mathematics. It is proposed that the term "of high diameter" can be used to describe groups with a diameter that scales exponentially prior to polynomially, indicating a distinct group of finite groups. A necessary condition for a group of high diameter is established, and it is discovered that such groups have only one conjugacy class of elements with a specific property and are characterized by having numerous central elements. A group of high diameter is defined as having a diameter that scales exponentially prior to polynomially, specifically with a parameter that can be expressed as (log |G|)/δ for a fixed δ, and it is proven that only finite groups meet this criterion. It is also demonstrated that among finite groups of high diameter, only those with a specific structure exist, including bilaterally free groups and certain constructions derived from them. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor array was also tested in a 64-element matrix, demonstrating excellent scalability. Given its exceptional performance, the temperature sensor is an ideal choice for high-complexity systems featuring dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, such as multi-core microprocessors, many-core architectures, and embedded systems in aerospace technology. The design has been thoroughly evaluated and the simulation, layout, and measurement data are available at https://www.circuitsonline.com/en/projects/detail/temperature-sensor. The temperature sensor core has been patented in the United States with patent number 33597930. The research was conducted in the Nanoelectronics Group, Department of Information Technology, at Brawa University. The temperature sensor was manufactured in the Nanosys Laboratory, a collaboration between Brawa University and Infineon Technologies AG. The research was supported by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education in Poland, the Centre for Research, the Brawa University Research Scheme, and the European Regional Development Fund in Poland. Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Ultimately, it may facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the complex relationship between the mass distribution of cores and the formation of massive stars. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The validity of our "leverage rule" has been confirmed through calculations of stress distributions on the basis of geometrical analysis. The stick-slip regime is characterized by a stress magnitude greater than on smooth surfaces, while the stationary regime is marked by stresses lower than expected, given the surface roughness. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The study of liquid foam interfaces can provide valuable knowledge for the understanding of other interfacial flows involving complex liquids. The presence of surface asperities was found to impact the orientation of plateaus borders, leading to a greater amount of border curvature in areas between large asperities. The curvature of the borders exhibits a power-law relationship with the distance from the center of the interface. The distribution of border curvatures follows a logarithmic function of the surface area per border, indicating that the distribution is unaffected by the size of the asperities. The power-law relationship between the curvature of the borders and the distance from the center of the interface holds even when the interface is subjected to stress, as observed through the formation of T1 junctions. The curvature of the borders also exhibits a power-law relationship with the height of the T1 junctions, as well as with the distance from the top of the T1 junctions to the center of the interface. The study has further implications for the dynamics of liquid foams, including the movement of plateaus borders and the formation of T1 junctions. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Furthermore, we discovered that the anomaly class's detection is straightforward, and the remaining classes are difficult to distinguish. Nonetheless, the difficulty in distinguishing certain classes is resolved by considering the Anomaly Score, and others require metadata. In the benchmark without considering the anomaly class, our approach ranks 13th out of 29 submissions. Nonetheless, we believe that further improvement is possible by refining the ensemble of CNN classifiers. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The connection between the elastic membrane's properties and a particular natural scale, tied to the circulation of fluid within the Hele-Shaw cell, also implies the presence of a universal scaling that characterizes the relationship between the membrane's elasticity and the size of the developed finger. The circulation of fluid within the Hele-Shaw cell significantly influences not just the membrane's state but also its entire system, as it shapes not just the condition of the membrane but also the condition of the surrounding fluids. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. In particular, the look-ahead attention mechanism leads to a significant 8.1% reduction in BLEU score reversal error, and a 1.0 BLEU score gain on the standard NIST Chinese-to-English translation task. This achievement is achieved with only 10% increased computational cost. Our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is straightforward and efficient, and our results suggest that it is a important feature that should be integrated into attention models for neural machine translation. Our code is available at https://github.com/sojel/look-ahead-attention. Moreover, a simple look-ahead attention-based generator is provided as a strong baseline for future research on target word generation relationships, see our paper for further discussion. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Furthermore, we illustrate the benefits of this approach by discussing the notable advantages that grid computing and the Globus Toolkit gained as a result of this methodology. In addition, we outline the lessons that can be learned from its development, including the significance of grid computing being viewed as a application rather than just a technology, and the vital role that job queues and a universal gateway played in its success. Finally, we discuss the suitable research areas and potential future developments in this field. Additionally, we present a hypothetical project that demonstrates the applications of translational computer science using an actual example. We hope that this approach will stimulate further research and publication related to the field of translational computer science. Despite the advantages of a translational perspective, we observe that publishing research in computer science often involves separating technical and applied aspects of work. Consequently, we propose some guidelines that encourage integrating both aspects and discuss some suitable research areas that can result from this integration, such as publishing application pathways for universal grid portability, and providing a grid computing curriculum. Finally, we share some overall thoughts about the field of translational computer science, emphasizing its value, the variety of projects it can involve, and the potential benefits it can bring to the community. We hope that our effort will inspire further engagement with this approach, as evidenced by the growing interest in related concepts like reproducible research and open science. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our analysis of its parameters through the Markov chain Monte Carlo method confirms that it satisfies all the constraints derived from the observed rates of cosmic expansion, the ages of old stars, the temperature and density of the cosmic microwave background, and the evolution of supernovae. Our results from plotting a set of cosmological parameters against each other reveal that this model satisfies all the requirements necessary to describe the observed evolution of the cosmos successfully. The model's predictions for the future of the cosmos are similar to those predicted by a constant dark energy density, which results in a finite time limit when looking at the model's evolution. However, the model's uniqueness sets it apart from all other dark energy models. The model's reliability has been assessed through the application of the Kolmogorov-Simonov test to a set of cosmological parameters, which demonstrates that the model's parameters evolve randomly according to the laws of a Markov chain. The model's ability to be observed has been validated by conducting a statistical analysis of the cosmological parameters. The model's future predictions include a universe that will end in a big rip if the model's viscosity coefficient remains constant. However, if the model's viscosity coefficient decreases, the model could result in a universe that will experience a finite-time instability instead of the big rip phase.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This involved increasing the diameter of the plasma chamber from 0.4 to 0.8 meter, which also improved particle power balance at lower electric fields. It was found that despite increasing chamber size, plasma density increased by a factor of three when it was operated in helicon mode, and other parameters also showed significant improvement. It is anticipated that IShTAR will be used to study plasma interaction with radio frequency waves in plasma border regions, and by adjusting the plasma source, it will be possible to simulate plasma conditions found in the edge regions of tokamaks. This will involve reducing plasma density by a factor of ten, which will require further reduction of the plasma chamber size, but it is believed that it will still be possible to achieve helicon mode discharge. If this is possible, it will confirm that helicon mode is a reliable mode of plasma production in plasma border regions, and it will also be necessary for the successful operation of the MAST central solenoid plasma cleaning configuration. Key findings from the study have been presented in various conferences, but it is necessary to document the detailed analysis of the data collected during the experiment. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, this approach provides a feasible solution for automatically detecting and counting nested structures, which has implications for a wider range of applications. Experimentation with this approach on public datasets shows that it exhibits superior performance, alongside more efficient computation, compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. To evaluate the practical effectiveness of this approach in real-world scenarios, it was applied to a series of challenging biopsy images and matched the results with gold-standard annotations obtained through manual annotation by pathologists. The resulting differences were found to be insignificant, indicating that this approach is suitable for use in actual cancer diagnosis protocols. Moreover, to further demonstrate the versatility of this approach, it was experimented with on another publicly available dataset, alongside a notable improvement in performance. The code for this approach has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address specified in the paper contact information. Experimentation with this approach has been conducted in conjunction with pathology professionals at the Department of Pathology, University of Helsinki, and has been proven to meet their requirements for cell detection in biopsy images. Furthermore, due to the limited image resolution that biopsy images typically entail, the challenge of detecting nested structures is relatively manageable with this approach, thereby making its practical application feasible in real-world cancer diagnosis settings. The approach presented in this research has been evaluated using public datasets such as CPM

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A demonstration of GCNN's versatility is shown by applying it to a handwritten digit recognition task using a non-trivial, randomly generated graph, resulting in a accurate and efficient classification system. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/Yue-Hsu/GCNN-demo.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Consequently, VSSA appears poised to enhance elastography imaging, particularly in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement, and offers a promising approach for improving other SA-based elastography techniques. Elastography imaging depth can be up to 20 mm in rabbit muscle tissue using VSSA. Furthermore, the technique has significant potential for imaging tissues with deep embedded lesions. The VSSA technique in this study was implemented using a research ultrasound system, yet the proposed method itself is a algorithmic approach, suitable for software-based beamforming technologies, such as field-programmable gate arrays, making it feasible for integration into ultrasound systems. The technique's advantages include improved lateral resolution, increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without the need for interpolation, and the ability to focus the beam without needing a receive coil. The research indicates that the technique can be used to enhance other SA-based elastography techniques, especially those employing dedicated ultrasound systems, such as siemens, Philips, or Biojet, via software integration. The outcome of this study motivates further investigation into the combination of VSSA with other elastography techniques, such as magnetic resonance elastography, as well as the application of the method to clinical scenarios. Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This is particularly useful for addressing decisions within interactive systems, as it allows the inclusion of predictive elements through the use of forward operators, which are capable of inferring new facts from existing ones. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. A thorough examination of various approaches to address issues of double counting and kinematic rejection in the context of W/Z PDFs and effective EW processes is also presented. A key finding of this study is the successful implementation of a simple cut-off-based double counting avoidance method, which is found to be effective for both universal and near-universal adjustments, and is amenable to integration into existing event generators through effective cross-section weights. A necessary condition to employ W/Z PDFs successfully is also identified as the energy level at which the relative deviation between W/Z PDFs and the standard approach should be below 10%, varying between 5-20 TeV based on the specific W/Z interaction and particle polarization. A comprehensive appendices section is also provided, covering vital details on W/Z PDFs, including their derivation, implications, and key properties. The research underlying this presentation has been featured in two previous publications, specifically the effective W/Z PDF research presented in References [1, 5]. The relevant research on the effective development of the collinearity region for W/Z interactions in the context of a muon collider was published in References [3, 4]. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We demonstrate how the ingredients and proofs of these theorems interconnect, building ultimately towards a stronger form of the first incompleteness theorem. We also examine some historical context and an illustrative application of these theorems in the framework of self-referential propositions. Finally, we consider possible extensions to a second-order arithmetic, and show that the principles of the first incompleteness theorem can be derived from the most basic axioms of second-order arithmetic via a more intuitive self-referential argument. We conclude by discussing the limited scope of the theorems with regard to systems possessing additional powers, such as a powerful enough consistency statement or the ability to enumerate the indices of its own axioms, and provide an illustrative example of how the theorems do not preclude the existence of an incomplete yet extensive system like ZFC. We also examine the relationship between the principles of the first incompleteness theorem and the capacity of a system to accommodate self-referential constructs within the system itself, as well as the underlying assumptions necessary to guarantee the existence of meaningful self-referential propositions within the system. Finally, we consider the most weakly consistent theory that satisfies the requirements of the first incompleteness theorem, and provide an appendix detailing the relevant technical proofs. We hope that this synthesis, historical examination, and analysis of the first incompleteness theorems, as well as their extensions, will serve as a useful resource for both researchers and students within the field. We also hope that it will help to demystify the theorems for non-logicians by emphasizing the underlying, intuitive principles and simple, recursive techniques that form the foundation of these celebrated results. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between these theorems and previous work by different authors. Our proof of the three balls theorem relies on an equation linking the Dirac operator, the Laplacian, and a scalar multiple (λ) which enables us to connect these theorems to classic results from spectral theory, thereby ensuring the validity of the three balls theorem for extensive classes of functions. Ultimately, our contributions lay the groundwork for extending Hadamard's three circles theorem to other monogenic functions within R^n+1 space, including those satisfying specific growth conditions, as well as polynomials and harmonic polynomials. Our approach also provides novel estimates of the growth of these functions along geodesic lines within R^n+1 space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these growth estimates converge at a rate proportional to (1 + λ^n)^k for both polynomials and harmonic polynomials, whereas they converge at a rate of (1 + λ^2)^k for certain classes of functions resulting from the composition of monogenic functions with complex variables. Our research on the geodesic growth within R^n+1 space also leads to the extension of the classical results established by Hansen, Leighton, and Vainstein for the Laplacian to the Dirac operator. Our study reveals that these operators share the same set of eigenvalues, in addition to sharing the same number of positive eigenvalues (in the case of the Dirac operator) or zero eigenvalues (in the case of the Laplacian), while also exhibiting the same growth rates for these eigenvalues, as well as the same dimension-dependent growth rates for both polynomials and harmonic polynomials. Our research has been published in the paper "The Three Balls Theorem in Clifford Analysis" which can be accessed at [1]. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, because GANs tend to be noisy and dependent on specific training data, we regularized the model to reduce this noise and ensure consistency across samples from different datasets. More importantly, we extracted a numerical quantity that represents the complexity of the model, which can be utilized for a 20-fold decrease in complex model dimensions before using a fixed simple encoder, resulting in improved performance and reduced risk of model collapse. We also introduced a new way to calculate the Wasserstein distance between probability distributions that can be used for evaluating the performance of sampling methods, along with sample inequality coefficients that serve as a measure of quality for sampled images. Ultimately, our approach led to a significant improvement in sampling from the posterior distribution when comparing it to current state-of-the-art methods, especially in scenarios with large model dimensions. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/WASPI.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Consequently, we emphasize the importance of distinguishing between these invariant configurations and the dynamically changing behavior observed in fractional-order systems. Ultimately, our discussion highlights the distinct challenges and possibilities presented by these unconventional systems. We also review the available numerical software and provide recommendations for future research on the subject. Additionally, we present a solved example and an unknown problem related to the dynamics of fractional-order systems. Finally, we touch on the potential applications and challenges associated with these systems, particularly in modeling real-world scenarios and the need for further mathematical and numerical research. Despite the obstacles they pose, these systems have the potential to accurately model and capture complex dynamics observed in nature and in various technological contexts, including cultural complex network systems and neural networks. We hope this article contributes to a deeper understanding of these systems and the importance of studying their dynamics. We also highlight the need for further numerical and theoretical research on these systems, with a view to making their dynamics more accessible and easier to analyze. We believe that this agenda is crucial for unlocking the full potential of these systems and for accurately modeling the intricate phenomena observed in nature and technological setups using models of fractional order. We propose that this agenda has the potential to lead to groundbreaking insights and innovations in various fields of science and technology. We also emphasize that the study of these systems presents a unique teaching opportunity to demonstrate the importance of mathematical rigor in numerical methods and the need for robust and accurate numerical software to analyze complex dynamical systems. We propose that this agenda could be achieved through collaborative efforts between mathematicians and experts in various fields of application, as well as through the development of suitable numerical tools and the creation of educational content to support the instruction of courses related to the dynamics of fractional-order systems. We also suggest that researchers consider publishing the numerical code used in publications in order to promote reproducibility in research and to contribute to the development of a community dedicated to the study of these systems. We envision this community as one that is interconnected, inclusive, and dedicated to addressing the methodological challenges facing the field, as well

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is a planar feature rather than a spherical cloud, and its orientation is nearly perpendicular to the line of sight to the pulsar, thus offering valuable insights into the three-dimensional structure of the interstellar medium that affects the pulsar. Notably, the void associated with this screen shows a spatial relationship with the pulsar, and theories about the origins of screening features in the interstellar medium suggest some may result from the gravitational influence of nearby stars or stellar remnants, potentially explaining the screen around PSR B1133+16. However, more research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis. This discovery also highlights the capability of long-term pulsar scintillation observations to reveal the detailed properties of screening features in the interstellar medium, revealing a screen's internal structure and precise location, and potentially revealing relationships between pulsars and their surrounding environments. This study's results will also be compared with future high-resolution mapping of the interstellar medium using next-generation telescopes. This research is the most comprehensive analysis of a single pulsar's scintillation pattern to date, and it provides a comprehensive understanding of the screening feature in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16, a phenomenon that likely exists for several decades. This paper presents the findings of a lengthy observation period of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, spanning 34 years, consisting of around 2600 recorded days through radio telescopes in West Virginia and Arecibo in Puerto Rico, observing scintillation patterns caused by the interference of the interstellar medium with the pulsar's electromagnetic signals. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to unsupervised music pitch change analysis and accurate prediction of pitch change probabilities. The model's effectiveness is attributed to PDCNNs' ability to adapt to novel frequency components and the cascaded design's capability to capture both long- and short-term signal dependencies necessary for quasi-periodic signal representation. The proposed QPNet architecture provides a versatile framework for a wide range of applications involving audio waveform generation from partial frequency information. The code for QPNet is available at this link https://github.com/ChenLiangCheng/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet. The audio examples and model parameter analysis can be found in the supplementary materials. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this approach leads to an expansion of the known classical results regarding the invariance of shadows, as well as advancements in identifying shadows for categories of modules and modules over rings with duality. The underlying theory of shadows can be applied to a broad range of contexts, including the examination of morphisms associated with algebraic K-theory, especially functors connected to algebraic K-theory, such as Waldhausen's functors and the THH of the category of modules. The framework of shadows also enables the creation of shadow structures for categories of modules that possess certain dual properties, leading to accessible expressions for calculating homotopy functors like THH and the Deligne- Lefschetz operator. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced for public use.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to GCNs in Euclidean geometry while requiring significantly less training data. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at IJCAI 2023. Experimental evaluations have been expanded to include two additional datasets, and the results shown have been updated to reflect the revised hyperbolic GCN architecture. Furthermore, LGCN's neighbor selection method has been enhanced, and the code is now available openly for public use. Despite the paper's expansion, the underlying research remains essentially the same as its original version. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this method allows us to solve the inverse problem through the use of a regularization technique. The solution to the source term is obtained by combining the classical Tikhonov regularization with a finite-dimensional decomposition. The effectiveness of this source term reconstruction method is demonstrated through numerical results presented in the study. In addition, the researchers who contributed to this work also established a connection between its components and several existing results, notably achieving the same stability estimate using only one measurement of the boundary values without requiring any additional information about the source term, thereby improving upon a previous stability estimate achieved in a separate problem. In addition, the researchers discovered that by utilizing multiple boundary measurements, the same structure can be used to obtain improved source regularization in comparison to using a single measurement only. Furthermore, the minimal number of measurements required to obtain the same stability estimate as achieved in a previous problem was determined to be one specific quantity, which is discussed in the study. The researchers also established and numerically validated a source entropy method that can be used to prove the uniqueness of the source term within the same structural acoustic PDE model, albeit with an additional assumption of time-reversal symmetry. The validity of this time-reversal symmetry was visually confirmed in a numerical example. The entropy method the researchers employed is distinct from the Carleman estimate approach used in the initial uniqueness proof. The relationship between the source entropy and the measurements of the boundary values was investigated, and it was found that a higher source entropy corresponds to a more distinct solution for the source term, while the source entropy also remained relatively stable over time in both numerical and experimental settings. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model can be applied to value
learning through a parameter estimation method based on the Tsallis entropy, which
enables us to generate empirically supported examples and scenarios. Notably, our
model facilitates value learning by incorporating a risk-aversion component, which
we term the star ratio, through the Tsallis entropy, and this has implications
for understanding the cognitive biases underlying delay discounting. In addition, our
model exhibits the same hyperbolic delay discounting pattern observed in the
standard model, thereby ensuring its broad applicability to various domains. 
Interestingly, our model also presents a condition under risk-averse impulsivity, 
which we believe has predictive power, given the right parameters, to indicate 
changes in delay discounting behavior over time. 
We demonstrate the efficacy of our model by conducting value learning with both 
fixed and dynamic risk-averse impulsivity, and the results show that our model 
accurately reflects the outcomes of these experiments. 
Our model's advantages are characterized by its minimal set of parameters, 
simplicity, and the implicit inclusion of risk-averse impulsivity, which we believe
will be valuable tools and insights for the ongoing research on delay discounting.
We also explore the relationship between our model and the commonly used discount
functions, and the results reveal that it behaves similarly to the hyperbolic discount
function in the limit of low delay, while differing from the exponential discount
function in the limit of high delay. 
Our model's parameters can be estimated using a method based on the likelihood
method, which we have tested on extensive datasets, including those with varying
levels of noise, and the results show that our model accurately predicts the outcomes
of value learning tasks, even in the presence of complex dynamics. 
We have made our code and model results available for public perusal at https://github.com/strataseq/TsallisDDM. 
We conclude that our model offers a compelling explanation for the delay discounting
behavior observed in value learning tasks, and it provides a practical solution for
predicting outcomes with delay discounting

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The resulting formulation also exhibits a modified Goldplatt-Weinberg relation and displays improved behavior at the quantum level.  Furthermore, the harmonic gauge formulation facilitates the inclusion of a cosmological constant and yields a linearized massive gravity theory that is invariant under a modified de Sitter transformation.  The present formulation's advantages are realized in the context of the linearized massive gravity theory in the absence of a cosmological constant as well as the dRGA and new massive gravity theories.  The harmonic gauge's emergence also implies that the relevant equations reduce to the form encountered in the metric formulation, allowing the linearized problem to be solved using the same methods, while the non-linear problem requires additional considerations.  In the context of the linearized massive gravity theory in the absence of a cosmological constant as well as dRGA and new massive gravity theories, the inherent covariant harmonic gauge symmetry can be exploited to solve the linearized problem, and the resulting operator for the linearized perturbation reveals the same general properties as in the metric formulation, as the (1.1) relation for the dual operator also remains unaltered.  However, the non-linear problem is seen to be distinct from the metric-based formulation, with the harmonic gauge leading to a smoother behavior at root k2 = 0.  The relevant formulations, including the harmonic gauge formulation, the Poincar\'e gauge choice, and the fully general approach, are compared and contrasted with each other.  The paper also touches on related topics, such as the Fierz-Pauli formalism, the de Donder gauge choice, the harmonic gauge choice for the linearized Einstein-Hilbert action, and the occurrence of the vDVZ discontinuity.  Ultimately, the paper presents a detailed description of the harmonic gauge formulation of linearized massive gravity, offering a covariant and consistent framework that provides a viable alternative to the Poincar\'e gauge choice. For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Furthermore, the canonical thermal equilibrium state is found to correspond to a loxodromic dynamics, whereas both the semiclassical and high-temperature approximations result in parabolic dynamics. Nonetheless, despite the loxodromic dynamics appearing complex, the associated thermal equilibrium state remains real, illustrating that the associated complex symplectic matrix is pseudosymmetric. This investigation also uncovers the connection between the loxodromic dynamics and the Arrhenius exponential form that the classical thermal physics typically employs. Moreover, a distinct perspective is obtained from considering the composition of metaplectic operators, alongside an exploration of the pertinent classical structures, to uncover the underlying complex symplectic matrix that governs the thermal equilibrium state's behavior. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we propose that the analogy to negative numbers provides a valuable teaching opportunity to address potential misconceptions and deepen students' comprehension. The paper also suggests possible activities and extensions for students to engage with in the classroom. The proposed resources are designed to be accessible and adaptable for both initial physics lectures and more in-depth courses, including graduate-level studies. The associated Python code can be utilized to demonstrate the phenomena through interactive simulations using Jupyter Notebooks. The material presented herein can be incorporated into existing undergraduate courses or served as a foundation for creating new curricular content focused on thermal physics. The code and supplementary materials are available at https://github/negativetemperature. The report is intended to contribute to the ongoing discussion on creating teaching resources that effectively incorporate conceptual metaphors and analogies in physics education. The term "negative temperature" is often associated with misleading popular science content. Consequently, it is not uncommon for students to arrive at undergraduate physics courses with preconceived notions of this concept, which can be addressed by providing a clear, evidence-based explanation. The current understanding of "negative temperature" offers a compelling opportunity to engage students in a critical examination of their own understanding and promote a deeper appreciation of the subject by utilizing analogies that foster a richer, more intuitive comprehension. The implicit connection between mathematical and physical representations can be put to use in problem-solving activities. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we analyze the predicted photon rates for dark matter direct detection and evaluate the possible variations in neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude resulting from different dark matter density settings. Given the existing limits on the neutrino oscillation length, we establish the minimum energy range for the heavy neutrino sector and establish the pertinent parameter ranges based on the simplest scoto-seesaw model. This reveals the potential for this model to explain the characteristics of the seasonal modulation seen in the DAMA direct detection data, following the elimination of all major exclusions via dedicated searches. Finally, we outline the predictive capabilities of this model, including the energy range for the heavy neutrino sector, the magnitude of the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude, the dark matter direct detection photon rate, and the anticipated outcomes from ongoing and future experiments. This model also offers hypothetical explanations for the 3.5 keV X-ray line signal, in addition to providing a minimum amplitude for the neutrinoless double beta decay even if the search for the heavy neutrino sector is unsuccessful. This amplitude, however, can be significantly enhanced through the formation of the heavy scalar neutron condensate. This scenario is characterized by a unique self-energy contribution to the standard model fermion masses, particularly the neutrinos, in addition to their tree-level and radiative components. This can be compared to conventional theories generating the mass scales for the atmospheric and solar neutrinos. This scoto-seesaw model also meets the requirements for the correct electroweak symmetry breaking, in addition to fulfilling the criteria for the correct dark matter density and the avoidance of vacuum instability and the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude above the planned sensitivity of the CMBN-20

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, the small branching ratio of some orbital occupations can be attributed to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing rather than being an intrinsic property of the material. Moreover, this work hints that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing may be a critical factor in establishing non-Kramers doublet states and, thereby, influence the realization of magnetic phenomena in certain metal oxides. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the necessity of considering $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in the analysis of transition metal oxide electronics and magnetism. For some systems with complex orbital occupations, the relevant theoretical models may need to be revised, while for others, previously unexplained experimental findings may now be understood in a new light. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it highlights the significance of these findings in relation to genus-zero property predictions. Lastly, it presents an illustrative example utilizing genus-zero properties to analyze an combination of topological string theories known as ODE. It also offers an alternative derivation of the related mathematical equations, known as the differential equations of Euler operators, which form the basis of the ODE. It further reveals that the solution to these differential equations can be expressed in terms of mathematical functions called Givental's I-functions and Euler operators, which are interconnected through a process known as the theta-operator. It also explains that the relative I-functions for the associated mathematical variables can be connected through mathematical paths, which are defined by a set of mathematical rules, known as the beta-vertex. It also discusses the properties of these relative I-functions, particularly with respect to their integration, as well as their relationship to the initial mathematical variables and the associated mathematical functions, which include Givental's I-functions, Euler operators, and the theta-operator. It also explores the connection between these relative I-functions and the genus-zero property predictions. It also presents an analytical example, known as the P(X_g) example, which is used to demonstrate the applicability of these mathematical theories to physical scenarios. It also discusses the implications of these mathematical theories for the related physical predictions, particularly with respect to their consistency with the genus-zero property predictions. It also highlights the limitations of these mathematical theories as well as the associated physical predictions. It also presents an alternative analytical approach, known as the direct approach, which is used to derive the same mathematical equations, known as the differential equations of Euler operators, but through a different methodological approach. It also uses this direct approach to analyze the same P(X_g) example, but through a different methodological framework. It also uses this direct approach to investigate the properties of the associated mathematical functions, particularly with respect to their mathematical stability, as well as the associated physical predictions, particularly with respect to their physical stability.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for multiple interesting directions such as incorporating clinical information, developing a more efficient inverse mapping technique, and utilizing this approach for disease detection. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly suited for
experienced professionals in the field of spatial science, geography, landscape
architecture, and engineering, as well as researchers in social and medical
fields, among others. The guide that follows provides a comprehensive overview
of the application's features and serves as a primer for employing ViDaExpert
in various academic and professional contexts. The associated source code and
application are available for free public use under the LGPLV3+ license, and
the guide is available as a PDF for downloading, as well as in ViDaExpert's
help menu. The research presented herein is an adaptation of the original work,
with significant enhancements, presented at the 2022 AAG Conference, in the
session Innovations in Geographic Analysis and Visualization. The research was
made possible by the funding received from the Italian National Group of
Cognitive Science (Gruppo Nazionale di Intelligenza Artificiale) and the
University of Urbino. The ViDaExpert application and the associated guide
can be obtained from the website of the CogLabs Lab at the University of
Urbino. The current version of ViDaExpert is compatible with Windows 10 and
Linux Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, and the source code is available on GitHub at the
following address: https://github.com/CogLabsLab/ViDaExpert. The 3D viewer used
in ViDaExpert is based on the Three.js library, and the charts are generated
using Chart.js. The application's source code includes examples of data and
scripts to facilitate understanding of its functionality. The associated guide
includes a tutorial on creating the application from scratch, as well as a
theoretical section regarding the mathematical foundations of its features. The
research mentioned in this paper has an associated DOI: 10.1016/j.jcsp.2022.100
